high_priority_articles.title: Laos Expected to Scuttle ASEAN’s South China Sea Code of Conduct - The Diplomat – Asia-Pacific Current Affairs Magazine
high_priority_articles.summary: Laos Expected to Scuttle ASEAN’s South China Sea Code of Conduct  The Diplomat – Asia-Pacific Current Affairs Magazine

source_detail.name: The Diplomat – Asia-Pacific Current Affairs Magazine

high_priority_articles.full_text:
Throughout its year as chair of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), the Philippines has aggressively sought to push the China-ASEAN Code of Conduct (CoC) for the South China Sea to the top of the regional agenda and end the long and drawn out diplomatic saga, which dates back more than two decades.
The CoC is part of a long (and thus far inconclusive) quest to find peaceful resolutions to the many maritime and territorial disputes that persistently plague the sea lines of communications across a waterway that accounts for almost a quarter of world trade. A CoC would enable ASEAN to negotiate with China as a united entity, and after all that is what ASEAN is supposed to be all about: a centrist political and trade bloc that can represent the interests of 11 Southeast Asian states on the world stage through a rules based order.
It’s a process that does not suit China, which has done its best to belittle and intimidate Manila and specifically Philippine Foreign Secretary Maria Theresa Lazaro, who has demanded respect for international law while juggling heated diplomatic tensions and the ASEAN chair. Publicly, Beijing maintains its policy of non-interference and at times even espouses the virtues of potentially resolving maritime issues with Southeast Asian states through ASEAN. But behind the public spotlight, China has persistently used its proxies to obstruct and scuttle the CoC.
Cambodia was particularly useful in this regard. At the 2012 ASEAN Foreign Ministers’ Meeting, hosted by Phnom Penh, Prime Minister Hun Sen was signaling a significant shift in foreign policy toward China and the CoC was topping the agenda. The Philippines and Vietnam pushed to explicitly mention the ongoing Scarborough Shoal standoff and Chinese maritime encroachment in their Exclusive Economic Zones, but Hun Sen and his Foreign Minister Hor Namhong balked and declared that such disputes should be handled bilaterally.
For the first time in ASEAN history, no joint communique was issued at the end of the meeting. It was a major embarrassment for the Cambodians.
The CoC was effectively frozen, delays amid the COVID-19 pandemic followed, and whenever necessary Cambodia could be relied upon to do China’s bidding and scuttle the process.
That is what China wants; bilateral negotiations between individual states that enable it to reject international verdicts like the 2016 arbitral ruling on the South China Sea while protecting its expansive unilateral claims and military bases on artificial reefs.
China has also secured its state, military, and civilian investments along Cambodia’s limited coastline, but times have changed with the roaring days of the Belt and Road Initiative disappearing into the vacuum of history.
Given the colossal damage caused by online scam compounds, Beijing would prefer to exact penance out of Phnom Penh than scout for new investments, and the Cambodians, sources in ASEAN are saying, are not prepared to weather the diplomatic heat from blocking another effort to resolve the CoC.
Thus Beijing has considered and pressed its alternatives ahead of the 49th ASEAN Summit, to be held in Manila on November 16–18 and chaired by President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.
Myanmar could work, but it remains barred from ASEAN summits in retaliation for the ousting of Aung San Suu Kyi’s elected government in early 2021 by a junta led by current regime president Min Aung Hlaing. That could change next year.
Timor-Leste, ASEAN sources say, is moving rapidly into China’s orbit, but as the newest member remains unwilling to upset Vietnam, the Philippines, Indonesia, Malaysia, or Singapore on the CoC, nor to offend Cambodia after it shepherded Dili into the trade bloc.
That leaves landlocked Laos, an economic basket case in a region struggling for growth, and an absolute dependent on Chinese largesse. There are shades of the Khmer-Sino relationship from a decade ago now emerging between Vientiane and Beijing.
Late last month, China and Laos announced the opening of a Military Joint Support and Training base north of Vientiane, which has already earned comparisons with China’s development of the Ream Naval Base in Cambodia. Joint military exercises known as “Peace Train 2026” were held in September.
“Cambodia does not have the appetite for this,” said a Western source privy to CoC negotiations between ASEAN states over the last 12 months.
“It’s overwhelmed by the mess created by organized crime, the scam compounds and the conflict with Thailand. Phnom Penh is now moving closer to the United States and it just can’t deal with any more pressure. Myanmar, not yet; Timor-Leste, watch this space.
“Laos? Laos has been tapped by China and will have to defend its interests, and it’s the only country in ASEAN that Beijing can lean on, and it has been doing precisely that. Laos is going to shatter the Philippine dream of using the chair to pass the Code of Conduct. It’s as simple as that.”

high_priority_articles.title: Malaysian exports to US surge 69.1pc to RM282.07b despite tariffs — Johari - NST Online
high_priority_articles.summary: Malaysian exports to US surge 69.1pc to RM282.07b despite tariffs — Johari  NST Online
high_priority_articles.full_text:
KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysia's exports to the United States surged 69.1 per cent to RM282.07 billion in the first nine months of this year, despite additional US tariffs on some Malaysian goods.
Investment, Trade and Industry Minister Datuk Seri Johari Abdul Ghani said total trade between Malaysia and the US rose 39.6 per cent to RM378.70 billion from January to September.
"This strong export performance was driven mainly by a surge in demand for electrical and electronics (E&E) products, particularly semiconductors, following the rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) technology and data centres," Johari said in a written parliamentary reply.
He was responding to Amirudin Shari (PH-Gombak), who asked about the impact of US tariffs on Malaysian industries this year and efforts to identify new markets for small and medium enterprises (SMEs).
Johari said Malaysia had also benefited from an exemption from additional US tariffs on most semiconductor and E&E products.
What To Read Next
"This decision by the US underscores the reliance of the US supply chain on the E&E sector."
The E&E sector accounts for about 64.2 per cent of Malaysia's exports to the US, with semiconductors making up 44 per cent of E&E exports.
Johari said the ministry had identified products heavily reliant on the US market that were subject to additional tariffs and did not qualify for exemptions.
The US accounts for about 32 to 47 per cent of Malaysia's exports of rubber gloves, furniture and medical devices.
Exports of rubber gloves to the US fell 1.6 per cent to RM5 billion from RM5.1 billion a year earlier.
Furniture exports declined 19.2 per cent to RM3.77 billion from RM4.67 billion, while medical device exports dropped 12 per cent to RM8.74 billion from RM9.93 billion.
He said some key industries had come under pressure to absorb additional tariff costs or offer discounts to buyers to remain competitive and retain access to the US market.
Diversifying export destinations and reducing reliance on any single market remained the best way to limit exposure to external shocks, he said.
The ministry was pursuing free trade agreements and exploring non-traditional markets in the Middle East, Africa, Latin America and South Asia.
It was also supporting SMEs through grants, incentives and trade and investment missions.
Malaysia's rubber glove exports recorded growth in several non-traditional markets, including Oman (712 per cent), Brazil (84.6 per cent), Sweden (80.8 per cent), Denmark (48.1 per cent), the Netherlands (43.7 per cent), Estonia (34 per cent) and Canada (18.4 per cent).
Medical device exports also increased in South Korea (206 per cent), Singapore (74.9 per cent), Sweden (65 per cent), Brazil (59.1 per cent), Türkiye (43.9 per cent), Canada (26.6 per cent) and the United Kingdom (5 per cent).
Furniture exports rose sharply in Guyana (586.1 per cent), Taiwan (140 per cent), Switzerland (135.4 per cent), Vietnam (99 per cent) and New Zealand (68.3 per cent).
Johari said the ministry would keep monitoring US trade policy and act proactively to protect exporters and reduce the tariff impact on SMEs.
The US imposed an additional 10 per cent tariff on nearly all Malaysian exports on July 24 after a Section 301 investigation into forced-labour allegations.
Tariff rates from a separate US probe into industrial excess capacity have yet to be determined.

South Korea’s economy grew faster than expected in the third quarter as an artificial intelligence-fueled chip boom powered exports and investment, but a contraction in consumption underscored an increasingly uneven expansion that may complicate the trajectory for further interest-rate hikes.
Gross domestic product expanded 1% in the three months ended September from the previous quarter, the Bank of Korea said Tuesday, after growing 0.6% in the April-June period. That exceeded the median estimate of 0.8% in a Bloomberg survey of economists.
The economy grew 3.4% from a year earlier, compared with a forecast of 3.1%. This followed 3.7% year-on-year growth in the second quarter.

The Saudi-led coalition against Houthis said Tuesday it intercepted wave of ballistic missiles and drones targeting two regions in Saudi Arabia, as the conflict with the Iran-aligned group intensifies.
The Houthis launched three ballistic missiles toward Saudi Arabia's Eastern Region and four drones toward the country's Southern Region, the coalition said.
Saudi Civil Defense issued early warnings for a potential threat in the Eastern Region and in Kharj governorate, later saying the danger had passed in both areas.
Saudi Arabia has intensified its strikes on the Houthis since the group captured strategic areas along Yemen's Red Sea coast last month, advancing toward the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a key global shipping route for Gulf oil producers opposite the Strait of Hormuz on the Arabian Peninsula.
Earlier Monday, the coalition said it intercepted and destroyed three drones over the Riyadh region and southern Saudi Arabia, without identifying their origin or intended targets.
The coalition also announced strikes on Houthi positions in Yemen, saying it destroyed ballistic missile launchers, storage tunnels and a missile depot.
Coalition spokesperson Turki al-Maliki said the operations aimed to dismantle the group's ballistic missile network and disrupt its supply routes.
The renewed fighting between the two sides has shattered a 2022 U.N.-brokered truce that largely halted attacks between the Saudi-led coalition, which backs Yemen's internationally recognized government, and the Houthis, who control the capital Sanaa.
The escalation has also opened another front in regional conflicts involving the U.S., Israel and Iran.

high_priority_articles.title: Federal Reserve likely to skip rate hike despite elevated inflation - reflector.com
high_priority_articles.summary: Federal Reserve likely to skip rate hike despite elevated inflation  reflector.com
high_priority_articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Federal Reserve is expected to stand pat on interest rates Wednesday even though inflation has accelerated in the past couple of months as the Iran war has caused spikes in oil and gas prices.
The Fed's latest policy meeting concludes less than a week before the midterm elections, which have focused heavily on concerns about the cost of living and affordability. Consumers have generally soured on an economy weighed down by more expensive gas, groceries, and clothing, among other items.
The Fed, led by Chairman Kevin Warsh, wants to return inflation to its 2% target, which it typically does by raising its short-term interest rate. Higher borrowing costs, over time, can cool spending and slow inflation. The Fed raised its key rate last month for the first time in three years, from about 3.6% to 3.9%, in what many investors and economists perceived was a first step toward a renewed effort to bring down inflation.
Yet Warsh faces a host of challenges in achieving that goal. President Donald Trump slammed the Fed for raising its key rate last month, though he largely blamed the central bank's rate-setting committee, rather than Warsh, whom he appointed. And some of the forces driving inflation — specifically the rapid buildout of artificial intelligence infrastructure and higher energy prices — won't easily be tamed by higher interest rates.
At the same time, other parts of the economy are already being hit by higher rates, which were lifted by market forces, even before the Fed hiked last month. The average 30-year mortgage rate reached a three-year high of 7.4% earlier this month, though it has since slipped a bit. Higher mortgage rates have made buying a home unaffordable for 5 million more Americans since the beginning of the year, according to Oxford Economics, a consulting firm. Over time, Fed rate hikes can make mortgages, auto loans, and credit card borrowing more expensive, adding to Americans' sense that things like homes and cars are getting pricier.
After the Fed announces its rate decision, Warsh will speak at a news conference, where his remarks will be closely watched for hints about the Fed's next steps. He will likely repeat the Fed's desire for a “timelier” return of inflation to the 2% target. Some may view that as a sign the Fed will boost its key rate at its next meeting, in December, a move already widely expected by Wall Street investors.
If the Fed keeps rates on hold, Warsh will be pushed to explain why the central bank hiked in September but not this month. Inflation picked up in September, when consumer prices rose 3.7% compared with a year earlier. The increase was much bigger than the 2.4% rate in February, just before the Iran war.
And on a monthly basis, the consumer price index — the most widely-followed inflation gauge — rose 0.3% in both August and September. At that pace over a full year, inflation would rise much more quickly than the Fed's 2% target.
On Thursday, a separate inflation measure more closely followed by the Fed, the personal consumption expenditures price index, is forecast to have jumped 3.6% in September from a year earlier, up from 3.4% in August. Core prices, which exclude the food and energy categories, are forecast to have risen 3.1%, up from 3% the previous month.
Aditya Bhave, head of U.S. economics at Bank of America, said economists and the Fed have gotten too complacent about above-target inflation. Higher oil and gas prices will likely keep inflation elevated for several more months, he said, and rising diesel costs will elevate shipping prices for nearly every type of good, which could spread inflation more broadly through the economy.
“Unless the Fed takes this problem more seriously and stops essentially making excuses about inflation, I think we're not going to get back to 2% until the next recession,” Bhave said.
Warsh will likely seek to keep the Wednesday press conference relatively short. It was about 30 minutes last month. Warsh's predecessor, Jerome Powell, often held news conferences for about 45 minutes.
The Fed's policy meeting is part of a busy week for central banks around the world. The Bank of Canada will also meet Wednesday and is forecast to lift its key rate a quarter point, to 2.5%. Policymakers at the European Central Bank and the Bank of Japan are both scheduled to meet Thursday and are expected to keep their key rates unchanged.
For Warsh and the Fed, another key consideration is that the U.S. economy is growing at a healthy pace and unemployment remains low, at 4.2%, even if hiring is also sluggish. The government will report Thursday on growth for the July-September quarter, which is expected to reach 3%, according to a forecast by data provider FactSet. That would be up from 2.2% in the April-June quarter.
Many economists argue that solid growth is evidence that interest rates aren't particularly high and the economy could withstand higher rates to combat inflation.

high_priority_articles.title: FOMC Preview: Fed Faces Tough Rate Decision as Weak Jobs and Hot Inflation Complicate Outlook - Coin Edition
high_priority_articles.summary: FOMC Preview: Fed Faces Tough Rate Decision as Weak Jobs and Hot Inflation Complicate Outlook  Coin Edition
high_priority_articles.full_text:
- The Fed faces a tough rate decision as weak job growth clashes with persistent inflation.
- Markets expect a pause in October, but hotter prices keep another rate hike in play.
- Bitcoin, gold and US stocks await Fed signals and fresh PCE inflation and GDP data.
The Federal Reserve faces a difficult policy decision as it prepares for its October 27–28 Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting.
Weakening US employment growth is colliding with inflation pressures that are forcing policymakers to balance slowing economic activity against the need to bring inflation back to its 2% target.
The Fed raised its benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points in September, bringing the federal funds target range to 3.75%–4.00%. However, October’s economic data have complicated the outlook. Weaker-than-expected payroll growth has raised concerns about the labor market, while hotter consumer and producer prices have reinforced the case for restrictive monetary policy.
Economists broadly expect the Fed to leave rates unchanged at this meeting. A Reuters poll published on October 20 found that nearly all surveyed economists anticipated a pause in October, followed by another rate increase in December. Bank of America remains a notable exception, forecasting another hike this month.
For Bitcoin, gold and US stocks, the decision will be significant. The Fed’s statement and Chair Kevin Warsh’s press conference will also hint at the next policy move.
US Weak Jobs Data and The Pressure on Fed
The September employment report, released on October 2, revealed the US labor market was losing momentum.
According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, nonfarm payrolls increased by just 29,000, missing the 89,000 forecast. The unemployment rate rose to 4.2% from 4.1%, while average hourly earnings increased by 0.1% month over month, below the expected 0.3%.
Revisions further weakened the employment picture. August payroll growth was revised from 162,000 to 133,000, while July’s figure was revised from a gain of 21,000 to a loss of 10,000. Together, the revisions reduced previously reported job growth by 60,000.
The figures confirm a sharper slowdown in hiring than initially reported. Softer wage growth also points to easing inflationary pressure if the trend persists. For the Fed, weaker employment strengthens the argument against additional tightening, as higher borrowing costs further restrain business investment, household consumption and hiring.
One disappointing report does not establish that the economy is entering a recession.
Hot CPI and PPI Affect Interest Rate Outlook
US inflation accelerated in September, supporting the case for retaining restrictive monetary policy.
The Consumer Price Index (CPI), released on October 14, showed headline inflation rose 0.6% month over month and 3.7% year over year. Annual headline inflation exceeded the 3.6% forecast, while monthly inflation matched expectations.
Core CPI, which excludes food and energy, rose by 0.3% month over month, above the forecast of 0.2%. Its annual rate rose to 2.6%, up from 2.4% and above expectations of 2.5%.
Energy costs drove a substantial portion of the headline increase. Gasoline prices climbed 9.1% during September, accounting for more than half of the monthly CPI increase. Shelter costs also rose by 0.4%.
Producer prices delivered another inflation warning the following day. The Producer Price Index (PPI) for final demand increased by 1.3% month over month, compared with a forecast of 0.6%. Core PPI, excluding food and energy, rose by 0.7%, against expectations of 0.3%.
Persistent producer-price increases raise business costs and eventually feed into household prices. The combination of accelerating inflation and weakening hiring leaves policymakers with limited room to maneuver.
Another rate increase would reinforce the fight against inflation but add pressure to economic activity, while a pause would give officials more time to assess incoming data.
Will the Fed Hold Rates or Raise Them Again?
The October FOMC meeting will assess whether September’s rate increase provides sufficient control or whether steady inflation warrants another immediate move.
The baseline expectation is for the Fed to hold its benchmark rate at 3.75%–4.00%. PIMCO also expects a pause, while maintaining the prospect of further tightening later in the year.
Bank of America’s forecast for a 25-basis-point October increase highlights the division over the appropriate policy response.
A pause would not signal the end of rate increases. Policymakers would use the meeting to assess the effects of September’s hike and determine whether inflation is becoming more persistent.
Investors will scrutinize the statement for changes in the Fed’s assessment of inflation, employment and economic activity. The voting pattern will offer additional clues: dissent from officials favoring another increase would reveal the strength of inflation concerns despite the weakening labor market.
Why Bitcoin, Gold and Stocks Are Watching the Fed
Bitcoin and other risk assets generally benefit when investors anticipate stable or declining interest rates as lower expected borrowing costs ease financial conditions.
Recent market reactions illustrate how economic data generate different outcomes across asset classes.
Following the September employment report on October 2, Bitcoin traded above $87,000 before later moving toward $85,300 in the reported intraday snapshots. Gold also gained, while major US stock indices closed higher.
The reaction reversed after the CPI report. Bitcoin fell to around $81,900 in an early post-release snapshot, while gold declined and the Nasdaq Composite finished the session down 1.88%.
The October 15 PPI release produced a different outcome. Bitcoin briefly fell below $80,000 before recovering toward $81,000, while gold rose to $4,156.52 per ounce in a reported intraday snapshot. The Dow Jones Industrial Average, S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite all closed higher that day.
The recovery coincided with lower Treasury yields and a weaker dollar, while stronger retail sales also influenced the session.
These moves show how markets adjust as investors reassess rate expectations and weigh economic data.
PCE Inflation and GDP Will Shape the Next Fed Decision
The October meeting precedes two important US economic releases scheduled for October 29: September PCE inflation and third-quarter GDP.
The PCE price index is the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge. The latest available August data showed headline PCE inflation at 3.4% year over year and core PCE inflation at 3.0%. An October 26 forecast snapshot listed expected monthly core PCE inflation of 0.3%, compared with 0.2% previously. Separately, Barron’s reported expectations for annual headline and core PCE inflation of 3.6% and 3.1%, respectively.
The advance GDP estimate is forecast to show annualized quarterly growth of 3.2% for the third quarter, compared with a revised 2.2% in the second quarter. These figures remain forecasts, not actual results.
Because both releases arrive after the October meeting, they will not affect the decision announced on October 28. They will, however, shape expectations for the December meeting.
The combination of inflation and growth data will influence market sentiment:
- Cooler inflation, resilient GDP: Easing price pressures and steady growth would support risk assets.
- Hotter inflation, strong GDP: Persistent inflation and robust demand would strengthen the case for restrictive policy or another rate hike.
- Cooler inflation, weak GDP: Lower rate expectations could support Bitcoin and stocks, while growth concerns weigh on sentiment.
- Hotter inflation, weaker GDP: Persistent inflation and slowing growth would complicate the Fed’s policy decisions.
What to Watch After the October FOMC Decision
The October 28 rate decision will be the main market focus. Investors will also examine the Fed’s statement and Warsh’s press conference for clues about future policy.
Three factors will be especially important:
- Treasury yields and the US dollar movements will show how markets adjust expectations for future interest rates.
- Real yields and risk appetite will help explain gold’s performance and whether Bitcoin and stocks benefit from easier financial conditions or face pressure from economic concerns.
- The October 29 PCE and GDP reports will provide updated evidence on inflation and economic growth ahead of the December meeting.
In sum, the Fed faces a balancing act between steady inflation and a weakening labor market. While markets widely expect a pause, the statement and press conference will shape expectations for future policy. The subsequent PCE and GDP reports will influence the December outlook and set the tone for Bitcoin, gold and US stocks heading into November.

high_priority_articles.summary: Dollar-yen rises into mid-157 range as markets eye US, Japan policy ahead of FOMC and BOJ meetings  BigGo Finance
high_priority_articles.full_text:
According to the currency outlook published on the morning of the 27th by Gaitame.com Research Institute, the dollar-yen is expected to climb into the mid-157 yen range amid continued speculation over US and Japanese monetary policy carried over from the end of last week. Takuya Kanda, a senior currency analyst at the institute, set the day's expected range at 156.80-158.00 yen and said the pair is likely to hold firm in the upper-156 yen zone.
In Tokyo trading on Monday the 26th, Germany's October Ifo Business Climate Index beating market expectations lent support to European currencies. The index came in at 90.2, above the market forecast of 89.9 and the highest since May 2023. It was helped by the expectations component, which signals the outlook, rising to 91.6, its highest since February 2022. The Ifo Institute said companies assessed the current situation as somewhat worse but "a more optimistic outlook was evident," adding that "the economic recovery is continuing."
Looking at major markets, the Nikkei Stock Average fell 503.51 points to 62,189.65, while European and US equities were broadly firm. The NY Dow closed up 146.42 dollars at 52,361.58, Germany's DAX rose 229.19 points to 25,410.84, and the UK's FTSE gained 78.70 points to 10,769.06. In bond markets, the US 2-year yield rose to 4.7159% while the US 10-year yield edged down to 4.9884%, with flattening of the yield curve in focus. In commodities, NY crude fell 1.51 dollars to 101.76 dollars a barrel, while NY gold rose 30.50 dollars to 4,038.40 dollars a troy ounce.
The week's biggest focus is the US Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting scheduled for the 27th-28th and the Bank of Japan monetary policy meeting on the 29th-30th. As currency analyst Tsutomu Nakamura noted in the report dated the 26th of last week, both meetings are widely expected to leave policy rates unchanged, shifting market attention to hints on the timing and pace of future rate hikes in statements and press conferences. With participants wanting to see the outcome of the meetings, the overall market tone is prone to a stronger wait-and-see stance.
That said, the upside is not one-way. At the end of last week on the 23rd, the dollar-yen posted a gain of less than 0.1% on a closing basis, and during trading hours it briefly fell to around 156.08 yen. Yen-buying prompted by a sharp drop in the Nikkei Stock Average came first, and the decline was later erased amid a narrowing of equity losses and higher crude oil prices stemming from uncertainty over the Middle East situation. In a scenario where concerns about the outlook for AI investment reignite and global equities undergo a major correction, dollar-selling and yen-buying could still strengthen.
Among economic indicators released at the end of last week, Japan's September nationwide consumer price index (CPI) rose 2.1% year-on-year on a core basis excluding fresh food, matching expectations and accelerating from the previous month. Core-core CPI, which excludes fresh food and energy, came in at 2.4%, above the market forecast of 2.3%, supporting expectations for the Bank of Japan's policy normalization. In the US, the October flash manufacturing PMI hit 56.0, its highest in four years and five months, while the services PMI fell to 57.9 from the previous month, painting a mixed picture of economic strength.
In Europe, Moody's kept France's long-term sovereign credit rating at "Aa3" and maintained its outlook at "negative." However, the agency explained that the current rating assumes passage of the 2027 budget and an easing of interest rate and social tensions, leaving room for future downgrades.
Gaitame.com's published expected ranges for popular currency pairs for today are as follows.
| Currency Pair | Expected Range | 
|---|---|
| Dollar-yen | 156.800-158.000 | 
| Euro-yen | 175.100-176.600 | 
| Pound-yen | 209.300-210.900 | 
| Australian dollar-yen | 110.100-110.900 |

high_priority_articles.summary: The Houthis Continue to Threaten with Missiles—Has Saudi Arabia “Surrendered” to Iran?  Atalayar
high_priority_articles.full_text:
A statement issued by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and reported by the Saudi Press Agency (WAAS) noted that: “As an extension of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia’s role in fostering dialogue and regional and international peace, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs confirms that the visit by Prince Khalid bin Salman bin Abdulaziz, Minister of Defense, and representatives of the countries of the Mecca Mutual Defense Agreement to the Iranian capital, Tehran, to meet with senior Iranian officials, falls within the framework of the ongoing efforts by the countries of the Mecca Agreement, the Joint Defense Agreement, to de-escalate tensions between the parties to the current crisis, promote dialogue and diplomatic solutions, and support the mediation efforts undertaken by the State of Qatar and the Islamic Republic of Pakistan.”
However, on-the-ground reports and independent sources reveal that the visit comes after Riyadh realized the impossibility of militarily defeating the Yemeni Houthis, following unprecedented attacks by the Iran-backed group against the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia.
Saudi Arabia tops the list of countries with the highest military spending in the Middle East and among Arab nations, at approximately $83.2 billion in 2025, while the 2026 state budget allocated approximately 240 billion riyals ($64 billion) to the military sector, according to defense budget estimates.
Despite this, Saudi Arabia failed to counter the threat from the Houthis, who announced that they were targeting an air base and a naval base in southern Saudi Arabia with “dozens of ballistic missiles,” in addition to Riyadh Airport, where aircraft were taking off and landing, according to their website.
Disruption in Saudi Arabia
Houthi spokesperson Yahya Saif stated that the group carried out “three significant operations involving dozens of ballistic missiles” at Riyadh Airport, Khalid Air Base in Khamis Mushait (south), and the Southern Naval Base of the Border Guard Forces in Jizan, where “the strike was precise, causing several deaths and injuries among Saudi enemy officers and soldiers.”
The closure of Riyadh Airport following the Houthi attacks dealt a major blow to the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, as a major investment conference and other events were canceled. Residents were forced to find alternative ways to travel.
Saudi officials did not provide additional information when the AFP news agency inquired about the resumption of flights at the airport. However, the flight-tracking website “Flight Radar” showed a small number of departures and the cancellation of a large number of flights, while the International Automobile Federation (FIA) announced on Saturday that the 2027 Saudi Dakar Rally, scheduled to take place from January 1 to 15, will not be held in Saudi Arabia due to events in the region.
The Asian Football Confederation also announced on Sunday the postponement of the match between the Saudi Arabia and United Arab Emirates national teams, scheduled for Monday in Riyadh, as part of the third round of the Asian Champions League.
The Stage Leading Up to the Collapse
Political analyst Abdul Qader Abu Lim asserts that “thanks to the betrayals of the Yemeni Reformist Brotherhood Party—which has been co-opted into the current Saudi system—Riyadh’s decisions are being condoned, even as it suffers the loss of powerful allies.”
He noted in a post that: “The Houthis managed to shift the battle from the stage of ‘breaking bones’ to the stage of pushing the Saudi regime toward war on the brink of the abyss—which is the final stage of the war before collapse—and this is what prompted the Saudi regime to visit Tehran, perhaps in hopes of finding a solution there.”
For his part, Yemeni journalist Fikri Saleh Hamlan asked: “How can Saudi Arabia sideline its sincere allies in Yemen, the South, and the United Arab Emirates, and meet with those who launched their planes and drones against them?”
He asserted in a post that “what is happening is not political maneuvering, but rather total submission to the conditions dictated by opponents following defeat on the ground and the loss of a reliable ally.”
Pakistan played a dual role, serving as both a staunch partner of Riyadh and an indirect channel of communication between Washington and Tehran, but the fighting that has erupted between the Iran-aligned Houthi group in Yemen and Saudi forces is increasingly testing the extent to which Islamabad can continue to play both roles simultaneously.
According to Reuters, this conflict marks the first major test of the joint defense alliance signed by Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Turkey in August, as well as an existing defense agreement between Islamabad and Riyadh. Under this agreement, any armed attack against any of the three countries is considered an attack on all of them, but so far, the alliance has not been visible on the ground, while Saudi Arabia remains under fire from Houthi missiles.
Pakistani officials fear that Houthi threats could put Islamabad at greater risk of being dragged into the war following Iranian missile strikes against Saudi energy facilities earlier this year, according to Reuters.
The Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia put this agreement to its first serious test, at a time when Riyadh is trying to prevent the clashes from spreading to its vital infrastructure.
Sources reveal that the visit by the parties to the Mecca Agreement is not for diplomatic purposes, as the Houthi attacks forced Riyadh to seek mediation after it failed to deter the group controlling Sana’a.
A Blow to the Allies
Meanwhile, these developments come after the Saudi kingdom turned against its allies in Yemen. This affects the United Arab Emirates and local powers, following the sacrifices they made to secure the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia.
The United Arab Emirates and the southern powers—led by the Southern Transitional Council and its affiliated forces, such as the Security Belt, the Giants Brigades, and elite forces—played a pivotal role in the military and security landscape of southern Yemen.
Securing the southern governorates after their liberation was a major priority for the United Arab Emirates, especially since the temporary capital, Aden, and its surrounding areas experienced a significant security vacuum due to the war launched by the Houthi militia.
In 2016, the United Arab Emirates and local forces expelled al-Qaeda from Mukalla, the capital of Hadhramaut, after a year of control. The oil-rich province shares a direct border with Saudi Arabia to the north.
Following Saudi Arabia’s strike against its allies in late 2025, when southern forces were bombed, Erik Kalinak, Slovakia’s representative to the European Parliament warned that the withdrawal of Emirati forces from southern Yemen had created a dangerous security vacuum, threatening the world’s most vital shipping route—the Red Sea.
Speaking in the European Parliament, Kalinak noted that “when we talk about security, we simply cannot ignore the situation in Yemen. Emirati forces have withdrawn from the south and have just pulled out their last counterterrorism units, and this has created a dangerous vacuum in the world’s most important vital shipping route.”
In Saudi Arabia’s first test following the United Arab Emirates’ withdrawal, its forces retreated in the face of the Houthi group, which controlled only the western coast in the Bab al-Mandab area. Aden became a temporary capital with the landing of United Arab Emirates soldiers, who spearheaded the city’s liberation. The vanguard of the Emirati special forces participated in the liberation of Aden International Airport and in organizing the southern resistance forces against the Houthi militias and the Muslim Brotherhood’s infiltration, which enabled them to extend their control over the southern regions.

high_priority_articles.title: Houthis hit Saudi refinery as Iran warns of ‘devastating’ response to further US-Israeli attacks - Middle East Eye

high_priority_articles.full_text:
Yemen’s Ansar Allah group, known as the Houthis, said on Tuesday that it had struck Saudi Arabia’s Ras Tanura oil refinery, the kingdom’s largest.
The group’s military spokesperson, Yahya Saree, said a ballistic missile ignited a fire at the Gulf‑side facility, west of the Strait of Hormuz, though Saudi authorities have not confirmed the attack.
The Houthis have intensified strikes on Saudi territory since Riyadh hit Sanaa’s international airport in July, breaking a ceasefire and opening another front in the wider US-Israeli war on Iran.
Saudi Arabia sends almost all its oil exports through two main ports: Ras Tanura on the Gulf and Yanbu on the Red Sea. The Houthis have previously attacked Yanbu.
Bloomberg News reported on Tuesday, citing a source familiar with the matter, that Saudi Arabia had contained a fire near the Ras Tanura oil terminal earlier that day.
Separately, Saudi‑backed Yemeni forces said they had carried out 1,276 operations against Houthi positions in the past 24 hours as part of their “Dawn of Yemen” offensive.
Military spokesperson Colonel Majed al‑Nuzaili said the operations had “neutralised” about 382 Houthi commanders and fighters, without specifying how many were killed or wounded.
He added that the forces had destroyed or damaged 140 military vehicles and heavy weapons, as well as several arms and ammunition depots, and had struck Houthi command centres, defensive positions, reinforcements and supply routes across several fronts.
The US Embassy in Riyadh has told non-emergency government employees and their families to leave Saudi Arabia due to safety risks, an order first issued on 23 October.
In a statement on X, the embassy warned of possible further attacks on airports, airspace closures, flight cancellations and travel disruption.
'US inability to provide security'
In Iran, Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council Mohsen Rezaei met Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei on Tuesday, state media reported. Khamenei has not appeared in public since succeeding his father, Ali Khamenei, who Israeli-US forces assassinated on 28 February.
Rezaei’s meeting followed talks on Monday with members of the Mecca Alliance - Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, Pakistan’s army chief Asim Munir and Turkey’s intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin - as regional states are seeking to end the war.
“Washington’s inability to provide security guarantees has become evident,” Rezaei wrote on X on Tuesday.
“Security in West Asia must originate from within the region itself, and any foreign intervention must be prevented.”
On Monday, at a campaign rally in Corinth, Mississippi, US President Donald Trump defended the war as he faced poor opinion polls ahead of elections that could cost Republicans control of both houses of Congress. He repeated a Republican lawmaker’s false claim that “we didn’t start the war with Iran. Iran started the war with us”.
Trump also defended the war’s economic effects, saying he had expected oil prices to rise much higher.
“I was fully prepared to do it because we really had no choice. Should’ve been done a long time ago,” he said.
Trump said he had never supported ceasefire earlier in the year.
“We did a little ceasefire, which I never liked very much,” he said. “We wanna be nice, but it was just a waste of time as far as I’m concerned.”
He added that Iran had developed missiles capable of reaching Europe and potentially targeting US cities.
'An unstable regional system has been constructed on the entirely false perception that there is a fundamental regional antagonism between Iran and the Arab states of the Gulf'
- Badr al-Busaidi, Omani foreign minister
On Tuesday, Abdollah Haji Sadeghi, Iran supreme leader’s representative to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, said Tehran knew “the enemy’s vulnerabilities”. He warned that further US attacks would draw a “harsher and more devastating” response, according to the semi-official Tasnim news agency.
Sadeghi said “the enemy” had wrongly assumed that assassinating Iranian leaders and military commanders would turn public opinion against the government.
After failing militarily, he said, “the enemy” was now using psychological warfare to create “despair, stoking divisions, and casting doubt on resistance”.
Speaking in Cambridge during a diplomatic visit to the UK, Oman's Foreign Minister Badr al-Busaidi called on Gulf states to form a non-aggression pact with Iran, and end the region's reliance on a failed US security umbrella.
"Instead of a genuine security structure designed to maintain stable relations between the eight states of the Gulf, an unstable regional system has been constructed on the entirely false perception that there is a fundamental regional antagonism between Iran and the Arab states of the Gulf," al-Busaidi said.
"There is no such fundamental antagonism. There are problems, yes, of course. But the plain fact is that Arabs and Persians have lived in peace around the Gulf for centuries."

high_priority_articles.summary: Saudi Arabia offered Houthis $1 billion through Iran to stop attacks: Report  The Times of India

Saudi Arabia has reportedly offered $1 billion to Yemen's Houthi group under an Iran-brokered arrangement aimed at securing a ceasefire and stopping attacks on the kingdom, Israeli media reported, citing diplomatic sources in the Gulf.
According to the reports, Saudi defence minister Prince Khalid bin Salman travelled to Tehran for talks on a possible ceasefire with the Houthis. The proposed arrangement reportedly involved transferring $1 billion to the group through Iran.
One diplomatic source claimed that the Saudi minister had even brought the money to Tehran aboard the Hercules military transport aircraft he arrived in. However, a Saudi official did not confirm that any money had been transferred, the reports said.
The talks reportedly brought together Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin and Pakistan's army chief 
Asim Munir
, alongside Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, Supreme National Security Council Secretary General Mohsen Rezaei and senior officials from the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).
According to the reports, Iran offered to mediate between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis amid escalating attacks on Saudi airports and oil facilities, which have caused economic damage to the kingdom. 
Iranian attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz have also disrupted oil exports from the Gulf, adding to regional instability.
The Saudi foreign ministry addressed the visit in an official statement, saying, "The visit to Tehran by Prince Khalid bin Salman, the defence minister, and representatives of the member states of the Mecca Joint Defence Alliance comes as part of the 'Nato-style' alliance's ongoing efforts to de-escalate tensions between the parties to the current crisis, encourage dialogue and diplomatic solutions, and support the mediation efforts undertaken by the State of Qatar and the Islamic Republic of Pakistan."
A Saudi official, speaking to Israeli media, did not confirm the reported financial transfer but said that part of the dispute with the Houthis centred on the implementation of understandings reached three years ago.
Under those understandings, Saudi Arabia was to provide direct financial assistance to the Houthis as part of efforts to reach a settlement. The funding was intended, among other purposes, to pay public-sector salaries in areas under Houthi control and rebuild civilian infrastructure. In return, the group was expected to maintain the ceasefire and stop attacks on Saudi Arabia, the reports said.
In recent months, the Houthis have sought to justify their "attacks" by alleging that Saudi Arabia reneged on the earlier understandings.
However, the Saudi position reportedly remains that the kingdom will not agree to a new ceasefire under "military blackmail". Israeli media reported that Riyadh also opposed transferring funds to the Houthis before they returned territory seized from Yemen's internationally recognised government, which Saudi Arabia backs.
The reported negotiations come amid wider regional tensions involving Iran, the United States and Israel. Tehran has sought to strengthen its regional influence while promoting a security framework led by regional powers.
According to Israeli media, the Tehran meeting also marked the first official meeting between representatives of the Mecca Joint Defence Alliance and the Iranian leadership. The initiative reportedly took shape during the Pakistani army chief's visit to Tehran the previous week.
The reports said Iran was seeking to position itself as a regional diplomatic mediator while opposing US or Israeli military intervention in the region.
The reported $1 billion proposal, including the claim that the money was brought to Tehran aboard the Saudi minister's aircraft, has not been independently confirmed.

high_priority_articles.title: Why Saudi Arabia helped create its worst Houthi nightmare – opinion - World Israel News
high_priority_articles.summary: Why Saudi Arabia helped create its worst Houthi nightmare – opinion  World Israel News
high_priority_articles.full_text:
For other Middle Eastern governments, the lesson is not that military strength is irrelevant, but that it cannot substitute for political strategy.
By Amine Ayoub, Middle East Forum
Saudi Arabia’s wealth and advanced military arsenal were supposed to shield the kingdom from threats across its southern border.
Yet renewed Houthi attacks have exposed the limits of that confidence.
In October 2026, an attack on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport reportedly killed at least 13 people and wounded more than 300, while a strike on an Aramco administrative building in Dhahran caused a limited fire.
Houthi claims about other Saudi targets have not all been independently verified.
Even so, the combination of infrastructure risks and threats to Red Sea shipping shows how an adversary with fewer resources can impose heavy costs on a much wealthier state.
The Houthi movement, officially known as Ansar Allah, did not emerge overnight, and its rise cannot be explained entirely by Iran.
Its roots lie in Yemen’s domestic politics, religious competition, and regional rivalries. Saudi Arabia did not start the movement, but its policies helped shape the environment in which it grew.
The 2015 intervention gave the movement fresh grievances to exploit without eliminating its ability to fight.
For decades, Riyadh treated Yemen as a strategic buffer. Religious outreach became one instrument of its policy.
Saudi-backed Salafi institutions expanded into areas where Zaydism, a distinct branch of Shia Islam, had deep roots.
This competition did not make armed conflict inevitable, but it sharpened anxieties over identity and political authority.
The establishment of Dar al-Hadith in Dammaj around 1980 marked an important stage in Salafism’s spread in Saada.
Associated with Saudi-financed outreach, the center attracted students from Yemen and abroad.
To many Zaydi communities, institutions teaching a competing tradition threatened their established position.
Saudi policy was not the only driver, but it helped turn religious competition into a wider political issue.
The Believing Youth movement emerged in this environment. Founded in 1992 by Zaydi religious figures, it initially promoted religious education and cultural revival.
Hussein Badreddin al-Houthi joined in 1999 and helped shift it toward politics.
Its appeal reflected not only opposition to Saudi influence but also local grievances, underdevelopment, disputes over state authority, and dissatisfaction with President Ali Abdullah Saleh.
Many Zaydis did not initially support the Houthis; their expansion depended on political choices and alliances, not religious identity alone.
The conflict became militarized in 2004, when the Yemeni government moved against Hussein al-Houthi and his followers.
Six rounds of fighting followed in Saada through 2010. The campaigns failed to eradicate the insurgency and deepened hostility.
Hussein’s death did not end the rebellion; his brother Abdul-Malik eventually became its leader. The movement survived and portrayed itself as defender of communities neglected by the central government.
Saudi policy did not create the Houthi movement, but it helped intensify the conditions in which it grew.
Religious competition reinforced sectarian anxieties and weakened confidence in the state’s neutrality.
Riyadh was not responsible for every Houthi decision, yet it bears responsibility for the strategic consequences of its long approach to Yemen.
The decisive regional turning point came in March 2015. After the Houthis seized Sanaa in September 2014 and President Abdrabbuh Mansur Hadi’s government lost control of the capital, Saudi Arabia launched Operation Decisive Storm under Defense Minister Mohammed bin Salman.
Riyadh said it would restore the internationally recognized government. The campaign relied heavily on airpower and Western-supplied equipment, but tactical superiority did not translate into political success.
The intervention treated a complex local insurgency as a conventional military target that airpower could degrade into submission. Instead, it became a prolonged war.
The Saudi-led coalition’s air campaign damaged civilian infrastructure, while import restrictions, economic collapse, and fighting worsened Yemen’s humanitarian crisis.
The Houthis also committed abuses and repressed people under their control. Responsibility for Yemen’s suffering extends across the conflict’s participants.
Still, international criticism of the coalition’s conduct undermined the claim that military pressure would quickly restore stability.
The intervention furnished the Houthis with a powerful narrative of resistance to foreign aggression.
This framing did not excuse their authoritarian rule or domestic abuses, but helped them present the war as a defense of national sovereignty.
State collapse and captured government weapons gave them resources beyond those of a local insurgency. Fighting provided experience, and the prolonged conflict accelerated their adaptation.
Iran’s role grew increasingly important. Tehran gained a partner able to threaten Saudi interests at relatively low cost.
United Nations investigators have documented Iranian-linked technical assistance, training, weapons, and financial support for systems the Houthis could not produce independently at scale.
Yet the movement was not manufactured in Tehran. Its local roots, captured stocks, battlefield learning, and exploitation of fractured institutions expanded its reach.
Iranian support amplified an existing actor rather than creating one.
The imbalance is increasingly economic as well as military. Saudi Arabia has invested in aircraft and air defenses, while the Houthis have relied on dispersed sites, drones, missiles, and tactics designed to complicate detection and interception.
The attacker does not need to destroy every target to impose costs: uncertainty can disrupt flights, raise insurance premiums, unsettle investors, and force authorities to devote resources to protecting infrastructure.
Such effects do not mean Saudi defenses are useless or that every attack succeeds.
They show instead that defending a large, open economy against repeated low-cost threats is a different task from winning a conventional campaign, and one that demands political as well as military tools.
By the early 2020s, war’s costs pushed Riyadh toward de-escalation. Oman helped facilitate contacts, and the 2022 United Nations-brokered truce reduced fighting without settling Yemen’s political future.
Saudi-Houthi talks in 2023 raised hopes of a wider agreement, but bilateral understandings could not reconcile Yemen’s competing authorities or guarantee that the Houthis would relinquish regional capabilities. A pause was not a durable peace.
The renewed confrontation also exposes how fragile the diplomatic track remains. In July 2026, the United Nations envoy held meetings in Riyadh and Muscat urging de-escalation and preservation of the truce’s gains.
The new fighting shows that contacts have not produced a durable framework.
Without a broader Yemeni-led settlement covering security, governance, and economic priorities, ongoing local battles can again trigger regional consequences.
The dilemma is that neither pressure nor accommodation has yet produced a durable outcome.
Airstrikes can damage Houthi infrastructure but cannot settle who governs Yemen; a bilateral truce can reduce danger but leave rivals vulnerable and the movement armed.
Without monitoring, security guarantees and a political process that includes Yemen’s own factions, each side has reason to rebuild its position and prepare to fight again.
The consequences extend beyond Yemen. Threats to Red Sea shipping raise costs for commercial operators and draw outside powers into a locally rooted conflict.
Attacks on Saudi facilities challenge the assumption that expensive defense systems can protect every site across a vast territory.
Interception matters, but so do intelligence, resilient infrastructure, diplomacy, and a settlement that reduces incentives for renewed attacks.
Alignments are rarely permanent, and local partners may pursue goals that diverge from those of their patrons.
A policy designed to preserve influence can intensify rivalries, while war can give an adversary credibility, experience, and new means of retaliation.
The House of Saud did not manufacture the Houthis. But Saudi-backed religious competition aggravated tensions in northern Yemen, and the 2015 intervention gave an established movement further opportunities to mobilize and expand its reach.
Decisions intended to preserve regional influence helped strengthen a threat that proved difficult to contain.
Saudi Arabia can reduce its exposure through diplomacy and a serious Yemeni political process, but a ceasefire cannot endure if it leaves the country’s power struggle unresolved.
Wealth can buy aircraft and diplomatic influence; it cannot purchase consent or guarantee political success through force. Riyadh’s nightmare is not merely the Houthi arsenal.
It is that strategic choices helped strengthen an adversary whose consequences continue to outlast the policies that produced them.

This ongoing regulatory scrutiny is vital for maintaining user trust and ensuring a fair and safe digital marketplace across the continent, setting a precedent for how future DSA breach remedy situations might be handled.

high_priority_articles.title: South Korea Q3 GDP beats forecasts as AI chip boom boosts exports, investments - The Standard (HK)
high_priority_articles.summary: South Korea Q3 GDP beats forecasts as AI chip boom boosts exports, investments  The Standard (HK)
high_priority_articles.full_text:
South Korea's economy grew faster than expected in the third quarter as a global AI chip boom boosted exports and investments, advance central bank estimates showed on Tuesday, though domestic demand remained weak.
Gross domestic product expanded 1.0 percent in the July-September quarter from the preceding three months, when it grew 0.6 percent. It was stronger than a median 0.7 percent increase tipped in a Reuters poll of economists.
It was also higher than the Bank of Korea's forecast of 0.3 percent in August, when the central bank projected this year's growth at 3.3 percent. The economy is now seen growing 3.7 percent this year, if GDP in the fourth quarter stays at the same level as the third quarter.
"It is estimated that about half of economic growth is being driven by semiconductors," Lee Dong-won, director general of the Bank of Korea's economic statistics department, told a briefing.
Exports and investments are expected to remain robust in the fourth quarter, Lee said, adding that chip production volume will expand further next year while prices will continue to grow but at a slower pace.
Private consumption, which fell for the first time in nearly four years in the third quarter, will likely recover gradually, as dividend payouts by chip firms to their shareholders in the fourth quarter and bonus payments to employees in the first quarter of 2027 boost household income, Lee said.
Amid the global boom in AI investment, South Korea's exports topped US$800 billion in January to September, higher than last year's full-year record, and are on track to exceed US$1 trillion this year, which will make South Korea the fourth country to reach the milestone, after the US, China and Germany.
The Bank of Korea kept interest rates unchanged last week, after back-to-back hikes in July and September, but maintained a hawkish stance by upgrading its economic growth forecasts and remaining upbeat about the country's export momentum.
"Exports and investments are leading growth, but the downside is that private consumption remains weak compared with the overall growth momentum," said Park Sang-hyun, an economist at iM Securities.
"There could be short-term boosts, but it is difficult to expect strong momentum given labour market conditions and restrictive interest rates," Park said.
In a separate central bank survey released on Thursday, consumer sentiment fell slightly in October, as the outlook for household income and consumer spending weakened.
In the third quarter, exports rose 2.3 percent on demand for semiconductors, machinery and electric equipment, while imports grew 2.4 percent. Facilities investment jumped 4.1 percent, led by machinery such as semiconductor manufacturing equipment.
Private consumption fell 0.2 percent as financial services declined on a stock market slump and car purchases fell due to strikes at major automakers.

high_priority_articles.full_text:
Key Takeaways:
- The 15 October 2026 Diliman Dialogues argued that Southeast Asians must shape South China Sea peace and cooperation themselves rather than accept external narratives.
- Speakers rejected a forced China-or-U.S. choice, urging strategic autonomy, functional cooperation consistent with law, and recognition of the economic costs of strained Philippines-China ties.
- Divergences persisted over shelving disputes versus protecting UNCLOS claims, yet the forum produced practical steps on dialogue, a Code of Conduct, incident management and evidence-based policy.
Amid rising tensions in the South China Sea and intensifying major-power rivalry, the 2nd Diliman Dialogues, held on 15 October 2026 at the Philippines-China Studies Center of Diliman College in the Philippines, advanced a simple but powerful proposition that peace, friendship, and cooperation in the region cannot be dictated by narratives produced elsewhere. They must be shaped by Southeast Asians themselves.
The forum brought together scholars from China and from the five founding members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), namely Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and the Philippines. Also participating were Chinese Ambassador to Manila Jing Quan, former National Security Adviser Clarita R. Carlos, former Senator Anna Dominique “Nikki” Coseteng, lawyer-politician Atty. Raul Lambino, Filipino Chinese Friendship Association President Danny Sze, academics, and civic leaders. Held during the Philippines’ ASEAN chairmanship, the forum provided a rare platform for candid regional dialogue.
The event underscored the importance of regional agency in addressing one of Asia’s most consequential security challenges. It advanced the central message that Southeast Asia should not merely serve as an arena for great-power competition but should actively shape its own strategic future.
Why Southeast Asian Voices Matter
The South China Sea is Southeast Asia’s immediate neighborhood. Its fishers, coastal communities, and trading economies bear the direct costs of instability. Yet the region’s story is often narrated by actors outside the region.
Former Senator Coseteng, President of Diliman College, emphasized the importance of dialogue, mutual respect, and regional understanding. She argued that ASEAN’s future should not be defined solely by narratives produced beyond the region or by the preferences of external powers. Instead, Southeast Asians must help shape the conversation based on their own experiences, interests, and aspirations. As she observed, dialogue does not require agreement; it requires a willingness to listen, understand, and engage before passing judgment. In this way, dialogue itself contributes to friendship and confidence-building.
In his remarks highlighting the first anniversary of the Philippines-China Studies Center, Rommel Banlaoi, the center director, backed President Marcos Jr.’s “reset” in Philippines-China relations as a pragmatic way to ease tensions. He cautioned that the reset works only if all government departments, including the security and military establishments, support it in action. The reset rests on the view that the Philippines can firmly assert its sovereign rights in the West Philippine Sea while still cooperating with China, its “permanent neighbor,” and maintaining its partnerships with the United States, Japan, Australia, and others. He concluded that a truly independent foreign policy rejects the “either China or the US” dichotomy and makes the Philippines a bridge rather than a battleground, and that Southeast Asian voices should shape ASEAN-China relations, including the push for a Code of Conduct during the Philippines’ 2026 ASEAN chairmanship.
A Shared Strategic Architecture and the Rejection of False Choices
Ambassador Jing’s keynote address began from remarkably similar premises. He argued that Philippines-China relations have reached a sensitive juncture that demands prudence, balance, and issue-specific engagement. He stressed that bilateral ties cannot be judged simply as “good” or “bad,” noting that while maritime disputes continue to generate friction, cooperation in trade, diplomacy, law enforcement, and people-to-people exchanges remains robust. Calling for restraint in the South China Sea, he urged both sides to avoid provocations, manage disputes through dialogue, and prevent maritime tensions from overwhelming the broader relationship.
The ambassador highlighted expanding trade, tourism, connectivity, and law enforcement cooperation as evidence that the relationship retains significant strategic and economic value for both countries. He encouraged greater Philippine engagement with China, stronger investor confidence, and deeper people-to-people exchanges, while criticizing what he described as discriminatory actions against Chinese nationals and institutions.
On foreign policy, Jing rejected the notion that Manila must choose between Beijing and Washington, arguing that the Philippines can maintain constructive relations with both powers while prioritizing its own national interests. He concluded by reaffirming China’s commitment to regional peace, stability, and mutually beneficial cooperation with the Philippines and Southeast Asia.
Dr. Carlos supported this view when she argued that the Philippines must pursue strategic autonomy and overcome its security dependence on the United States. The logic of her argument is that a country reliant on a single security partner has less room for independent judgment, and that its choices in the South China Sea risk being shaped by the priorities of others rather than by its own national interests. As the way forward, she called for more functional cooperation in the South China Sea, meaning practical collaboration on shared concerns that does not wait for the sovereignty disputes to be settled.
Friendship and Cooperation as Foundations of Peace
Congressman Antolin A. Oreta III, Chairperson of the House Special Committee on the West Philippine Sea, described the accomplishments of the Committee and reaffirmed its commitment to advancing the Philippines’ maritime rights through legislative action in accordance with international law. He stressed that this legal and legislative track goes hand in hand with peaceful dialogue and practical cooperation with the other claimants. His message thus showed that defending maritime rights and pursuing dialogue are complementary rather than competing tasks, and it gave the Philippine legislature a visible place in the country’s approach to the South China Sea.
Atty. Lambino, speaking as President of the Association for Philippines-China Understanding (APCU), welcomed the Dialogues as a place where Southeast Asian voices have a seat at the table and argued that cooperation begins with understanding that comes “from the heart” (mula sa puso), so that friendship between Filipinos and Chinese is built through conversation, shared experience, and mutual respect rather than agreements and official visits alone. He devoted his remarks to technology, especially artificial intelligence, as the force that will shape the region’s future more than any other. Small and middle nations, he observed, have too often been the stage on which larger powers played out their rivalries, and those that escaped this pattern did so by building capability in their people, industries, food systems, and technology while keeping the freedom to choose their partners wisely. He pointed to Vietnam, Malaysia, and Singapore, which chose a balanced and independent course and were rewarded with progress as well as peace.
Mr. Sze, President of the Filipino Chinese Friendship Association (FCFA) organized his message around three themes: peace, friendship, and cooperation. He held that political differences between governments should not damage the friendship between the two peoples, and that the real question is how such differences are managed, whether allowed to grow into greater divisions or addressed through patient and sincere dialogue. He recalled two historical occasions, the 1986 meeting between Vice President Salvador Laurel and Deng Xiaoping and the 1988 visit of President Corazon Aquino, occasions on which Deng proposed setting the maritime disputes aside temporarily while exploring peaceful solutions and, later, joint development. Sze argued that protecting national interests and maintaining peaceful relations are not contradictory.
Taken together, messages by all speakers gave the forum’s central premise legal, strategic, and relational foundations. Oreta emphasized the legal and legislative defense of maritime rights, Lambino emphasized capability, technology transfer, and the freedom to choose partners, and Sze emphasized dialogue and joint development. Lambino’s call for a balanced and independent course echoed the strategic autonomy urged by Carlos and Banlaoi, while Sze’s invocation of Deng Xiaoping’s approach of shelving disputes closely paralleled Ambassador Jing’s advocacy of joint development, with Sze adding the qualification that any such framework must be consistent with domestic and international law. The messages also complemented Coseteng’s observation that dialogue builds friendship and confidence. Together they suggest that friendship is not a substitute for defending national interests but the condition under which dialogue, restraint, and compromise become possible.
ASEAN Centrality and ASEAN-China Relations
Under the provocative title “ASEAN Centrality (?)”, Carlos presented a skeptical assessment of ASEAN’s current condition. She pointed to the absence of a unified collective voice, the growing preference for bilateral over multilateral diplomacy, the constraints imposed by consensus decision-making, the limited capacity of the ASEAN Secretariat, intensifying major-power rivalry, and the reputational costs of ASEAN’s inability to address the Myanmar crisis effectively. Indonesia has officially reduced its natural gas pipeline exports to Singapore, trimming flows by 31 billion British thermal units per day (BBTUD) in a strategic move to prioritize domestic energy requirements. The reduction, which took effect in late October 2026, underscores a shifting energy paradigm in Southeast Asia as Jakarta seeks to shore up local industrial supply and support its broader energy transition goals. The move has prompted careful monitoring by Singaporean energy authorities, who rely heavily on imported gas for electricity generation.
The decision aligns with President Prabowo Subianto’s administration's push to enforce stricter Domestic Market Obligations (DMO) for energy producers. By retaining a larger share of its natural gas output for internal consumption, Indonesia aims to stabilize local energy prices, support downstream industrialization, and reduce reliance on coal-fired power generation. The export trimming is expected to last for a designated period, signaling a structural recalibration of regional energy trade flows rather than a temporary supply disruption.
Pipeline Reductions and Domestic Priorities
The reduction in pipeline flows affects the long-standing energy trade relationship between the two neighboring nations. Singapore imports the vast majority of its natural gas via subsea pipelines from Indonesia and Malaysia to fuel its highly efficient combined-cycle gas turbine power plants. The 31 BBTUD cut represents a notable percentage of the daily transit volume, requiring Singapore’s energy market operator to adjust its grid dispatch models and secure alternative supply margins to maintain system reliability.
Indonesian energy officials have defended the reduction as a necessary step to meet surging domestic demand, particularly from the manufacturing and petrochemical sectors. The government has increasingly signaled that future energy resource extraction will be heavily weighted toward supporting national economic development rather than purely export-oriented revenue generation. This policy shift reflects a broader trend among resource-rich ASEAN nations to leverage their natural capital for domestic industrial value addition.
Impact on Singapore's Energy Security
For Singapore, the reduction highlights the inherent vulnerabilities of an energy-importing nation with limited indigenous resources. The city-state has spent the past decade aggressively diversifying its energy import routes and investing in regasification terminals to accept Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) from global spot markets. While the pipeline reductions from Indonesia are significant, Singapore’s Energy Market Authority has noted that existing long-term contractual frameworks remain intact and that the national grid possesses sufficient buffer capacity to absorb the shortfall without disrupting consumer supply.
Nevertheless, the incident serves as a catalyst for Singapore to accelerate its investments in alternative energy sources, including regional power grids and low-carbon hydrogen. Energy analysts suggest that the gradual tightening of Indonesian export policies will force Singaporean utilities to lock in longer-term, higher-cost LNG contracts or accelerate the deployment of floating solar and regional subsea interconnectors to mitigate future geopolitical supply risks.
Contractual Obligations Versus Market Realities
The reduction has sparked complex discussions regarding the enforceability of cross-border energy contracts in the face of sovereign policy shifts. While Indonesian authorities maintain that the trimming does not breach the fundamental terms of existing supply agreements—often structured with flexible delivery windows and force majeure clauses for domestic emergencies—buyers in Singapore face increased procurement costs to replace the deferred pipeline volumes on the spot market.
Legal and energy trade experts note that sovereign resource nationalism is becoming a more prominent factor in ASEAN energy markets. Governments are increasingly willing to invoke domestic priority clauses to redirect energy flows, even if it causes friction with neighboring trade partners. This dynamic requires regional utilities to build more robust contingency plans and diversify their supply portfolios to insulate consumers from sudden policy-driven volume reductions.
Regional Energy Transition and Policy Shifts
The export curtailment also intersects with Indonesia’s broader commitments to peak power sector emissions and achieve net-zero targets by 2060. By prioritizing gas over coal for domestic baseload power, Jakarta is attempting to manage its carbon footprint while sustaining economic growth. However, the finite nature of its conventional gas reserves means that domestic prioritization will inevitably reduce the surplus available for export to neighboring grids.
- Downstream Industrialization: Retaining gas supplies supports the development of domestic fertilizer, methanol, and petrochemical manufacturing hubs.
- Grid Stability: Ensuring adequate baseload gas supply is critical for integrating higher percentages of intermittent renewable energy into the Indonesian national grid.
- Regional Pricing: Reduced pipeline exports contribute to tighter regional gas markets, potentially elevating long-term LNG benchmark prices in the Asia-Pacific region.
As Southeast Asia navigates the complex transition toward sustainable energy systems, the recalibration of cross-border gas flows between Indonesia and Singapore will serve as a critical case study in balancing national resource sovereignty with regional energy interdependence.

The Bank of Korea (BOK) announced on 27 October that South Korea’s real gross domestic product grew by 1.0% in the third quarter from the previous three months, beating a consensus of economists centred around 0.7% and surprising markets that had expected a sharper post-spring slowdown. According to the preliminary figures released by the central bank, annual growth came in at 3.2%, above estimates of 3.0% but down from the 3.7% recorded in the previous quarter.
The release validates the BOK’s bet on an export-led recovery at a time when the global semiconductor cycle is exceptionally supportive. A survey of economists conducted ahead of the data had forecast a pick-up in activity on the back of chip exports and AI-related investment, after a 0.6% GDP increase in the second quarter. For bond investors and banks alike, the key question now is how long export momentum can offset persistent weakness in domestic demand.
The breakdown of the figures confirms that external demand remains the main growth engine. Semiconductor exports were the principal driver of the expansion, with major chipmakers such as Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix benefiting from exceptional demand for advanced memory destined for AI infrastructure. Rising orders from data centres and compute-heavy AI workloads are reinforcing an industrial specialisation that positions Seoul at the core of the global semiconductor value chain.
A chip cycle that masks domestic fragilities
Behind the headline surprise, the growth profile remains unbalanced. Domestic sectors, especially housing and household consumption, continue to underperform, increasing the economy’s dependence on external demand for chips. For the BOK, which raised its policy rate to 3.00% in late August to contain inflation and financial stability risks, this K-shaped pattern makes it harder to arbitrate between supporting activity and managing household leverage. The monetary policy board delivered a second consecutive 25 basis point hike and simultaneously revised its 2026 growth forecast up to 3.3%.
The contrast is starker given how sharply the quarterly trajectory has already turned this year. Between January and March, GDP jumped by 1.7% quarter-on-quarter, the fastest pace since 2020, before slowing to 0.6% in the second quarter, a performance that already exceeded expectations thanks to strong exports of AI-related components. The third quarter thus confirms a high but more normalised pace of expansion, running ahead of the cautious scenarios many institutions had sketched out at the start of the year.
A stronger foothold in global semiconductor trade
The current sequence is consolidating Seoul’s role as a key hub for global semiconductor flows. Recent data from investment agency Invest KOREA show that in 2024 South Korea’s semiconductor exports reached USD 141.9 billion, accounting for 20.8% of the country’s total exports and standing clearly as its largest export item. In a context of surging demand from hyperscalers and major tech groups for AI training capacity, these volumes mechanically translate into a larger contribution to GDP.
More recent customs statistics confirm that this trend has accelerated in 2026. In August, total exports surpassed USD 98.25 billion for the third month in a row, led by semiconductors whose shipments surged 209% year-on-year to a monthly record of USD 46.65 billion. The combination of higher volumes and rising contract prices helps explain why the chip industry alone could deliver the upside surprise on growth.
What the GDP beat changes for the Bank of Korea
For the BOK, stronger-than-expected GDP growth temporarily strengthens the case for the gradual tightening path it has outlined in recent months. Local analysis suggests that achieving the roughly 3.3% growth rate targeted for 2026 remains compatible with quarterly GDP increases in the 0.4–0.6% range in the second half of the year; with Q3 now exceeding that band, the door is open to at least one further rate hike if inflation fails to ease.
In the coming days, the sectoral breakdown of GDP and the BOK governor’s remarks at the October post-decision press conference will be key to gauging whether the central bank frames this upside surprise as a one-off driven by the chip cycle or as the start of a more durable expansion underpinned by stronger domestic engines.
