The chip boom is feeding the public purse too: officials project national tax revenue to reach 478.6 trillion won this year - the highest on record - an outcome driven by booming chip earnings, one off dividend distributions, and brisk stock trading, and representing an increase of 28% from 2025. Seoul's plan for the coming year calls for a 12.8% increase in public spending, directing substantial resources to AI and chip infrastructure.
Prices, policy, and your portfolio
Inflation is still above target. In September, headline inflation increased 2.9% compared with a year ago; core inflation, excluding food and energy, was 2.8%. The BOK held rates at 3% last week after quarter-point moves in July and August, and Governor Shin says policy stays restrictive until inflation is clearly converging to 2%. Before the GDP print, Citigroup and Nomura penciled in 25 basis point hikes in November and February, which would bring the benchmark to 3.5%.
Why does that matter? If chip-led strength spills into wages and household spending, the case for more tightening strengthens. If it stays concentrated in tech profits, the growth impulse could be narrower. Either path will shape rate expectations, fiscal support for AI and semis, and how Korea's equity and currency markets trade from here.

high_priority_articles.title: The ASEAN-India Trade Agreement and Its Discontents - The Diplomat – Asia-Pacific Current Affairs Magazine
high_priority_articles.summary: The ASEAN-India Trade Agreement and Its Discontents  The Diplomat – Asia-Pacific Current Affairs Magazine

source_detail.name: The Diplomat – Asia-Pacific Current Affairs Magazine

high_priority_articles.full_text:
Even as India has embraced a renewed fervor for free trade agreements, one trade deal remains disfavored in Indian memory. The 2009 ASEAN-India Goods in Trade Agreement (AITIGA) is one of the oldest trade agreements signed by post-liberalization India as well as one of its most controversial. Atypically for an establishment that prefers to settle diplomatic disputes behind the scenes, Indian diplomats and trade officials are publicly trenchant in their criticism of AITIGA.
An oft-repeated narrative has emerged around the agreement: in the early 2000s, inexperienced Indian negotiators walked into an asymmetric deal, opening up their markets while getting little in return. Consequently, India’s trade deficit with ASEAN ballooned. Moreover, China exploited the AITIGA to route its goods into India through Southeast Asia.
This narrative stems from misremembering history. Rather than a powerful tool for ASEAN and China to penetrate the Indian market, the AITIGA is, in fact, a shallow and weak instrument. Moreover, it is shallow precisely because India preferred it that way. By repeatedly telling itself an alternative story, New Delhi has developed irrational fears over economic cooperation with Southeast Asia and injected unnecessary acrimony in the relationship. The myth of AITIGA as a bad deal is costing India diplomatically.
India started running a trade deficit with ASEAN in 1996, 13 years before the AITIGA was signed. The deficit stemmed from Southeast Asia’s shift from agrarian to manufacturing-led economies. The currency devaluations triggered by the 1997 Asian Financial Crisis further boosted the deficit. While the absolute figure of the trade deficit has ballooned over the last three decades, the India-ASEAN imports-to-exports ratio remains broadly similar to what it was in the 1990s.
After the 1997 crisis, ASEAN was looking to economically integrate itself with its East Asian neighbors. In the early 2000s, it began pursuing ASEAN+1 FTAs with its six immediate neighbors: China, India, Japan, South Korea, Australia, and New Zealand. India had been excluded from the first wave of post-1997 regional integration – the ASEAN Plus Three, Asian Bond Markets Initiative, and Chiang Mai Initiative for currency swap. Eager not to miss out on another wave of regional integration, India agreed to negotiate the FTA.
Contrary to the myth, Indian officials were tough negotiators. After all, India had decades of experience negotiating economic deals in the GATT, WTO, and elsewhere. The negotiations were tortuous and took much longer than the other ASEAN+1 FTAs.
Moreover, there was a mismatch of approach. On the one hand, eager to gain access to the Indian market, ASEAN wanted to widen the FTA’s scope. On the other hand, India looked to protect its domestic industry by limiting the scope of the agreement. Indian businesses were lukewarm about seeking out greater market access in Southeast Asia.
India’s tough negotiating ensured that the AITIGA was the shallowest of the ASEAN+1 FTAs. Whereas all other agreements committed parties to tariff elimination coverage of more than 90 percent, the AITIGA’s promised coverage hovered around 79 percent. ASEAN mirrored India’s reluctance to open its markets. For instance, Indian critics of the AITIGA often point to the fact that Indonesia promised only 48.7 percent tariff elimination coverage to India. Notably, Indonesia offered above 91 percent coverage to all other ASEAN+1 partners, including Australia, with which it ran a trade deficit at the time.
AITIGA also ended up with the most stringent Rules of Origin among all the ASEAN+1 FTAs. It is the only agreement that demands dual compliance (35 percent local content and change in tariff subheading) for goods to qualify for preferential treatment. Its complex compliance rules and lower scope resulted in exporters avoiding using the AITIGA.
In AITIGA, India got what it wanted – an agreement that signaled India’s commitment to its Look East policy without exposing its domestic industry to excessive international competition. While economists may argue over whether Indian protectionism is good economic policy, the debate is irrelevant from a diplomatic standpoint. For whatever reasons, Indian economic managers prefer shielding the Indian market. The AITIGA was a natural outcome of such preference.
However, to then construct a narrative of the agreement as a bad deal in which India got duped is diplomatically damaging. To begin with, it erodes India’s credibility in the region as a reliable and competent partner. India began criticizing the AITIGA almost as soon as it was signed. The two sides agreed to open a review of the agreement in 2015 but still haven’t concluded it. Such long-drawn, dangling processes chip away at India’s image.
AITIGA’s beleaguered state becomes a particularly bad look when contrasted with other ASEAN+1 FTAs, especially the one with China. Beijing began negotiating its FTA with ASEAN around the same time as New Delhi. However, it not only concluded the negotiations fairly quickly, but China and ASEAN have since upgraded the agreement twice. Today, the ASEAN-China FTA is a powerful instrument that deals with a range of issues from digital trade to green technology.
The narrative of AITIGA as a loss for India has made New Delhi a less confident economic actor in Southeast Asia. The resultant hesitation has been evident in India’s exit from the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership as well as its reluctance to conclude bilateral FTAs with Southeast Asian countries such as Thailand and Indonesia. Today, even as India seeks out FTAs in the Middle East and Europe, it is too unsure of itself to look for a trade deal in Southeast Asia.
Tellingly, the acrimony over AITIGA has spilled over into other aspects of ASEAN-India economic cooperation, even the ones which are in India’s interests. For instance, the 2014 ASEAN-India Trade in Services Agreement needs urgent upgradation to account for all the advancements in the digital economy. Given that India enjoys a services surplus with Southeast Asia, New Delhi should be eagerly driving the process. However, so far the two sides have not even begun discussing the issue.
The self-created myths around AITIGA have cast a shadow on India’s Look/Act East policy. New Delhi needs to shed them to become a more confident, credible and engaged actor in the region.

high_priority_articles.title: Egypt authorises military support for Saudi Arabia as Houthi militia attacks escalate - TRT World
high_priority_articles.summary: Egypt authorises military support for Saudi Arabia as Houthi militia attacks escalate  TRT World
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Egypt’s parliament has authorised the country’s military to provide support for Saudi Arabia’s defence, lawmakers and local media reported, potentially bringing Cairo closer to a regional conflict intensified by attacks from Yemen’s Houthi militia.
President Abdel Fattah el Sisi asked parliament last week to approve military assistance if Riyadh requests help defending itself against the Houthis, whose operations threaten Saudi territory and the strategic Bab al Mandab Strait, a vital shipping passage linking the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and access to Egypt’s Suez Canal.
The parliamentary authorisation comes as attacks on Saudi Arabia have disrupted aviation and oil exports, raising concerns over regional security and international trade routes.
Cairo draws a line around its military role
Egypt has repeatedly condemned Iranian and Iran-backed attacks on Gulf countries but has not publicly joined direct combat in the current conflict.
Sisi has indicated that any Egyptian support would be limited to defending Saudi territory and borders, rather than launching attacks inside Yemen.
Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty and intelligence chief Hassan Rashad travelled to Riyadh last Wednesday to deliver a letter from Sisi to Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman.
Following the visit, Abdelatty said Cairo supported exploring “every opportunity” to resolve the Yemen conflict through diplomacy.
Egypt’s potential involvement would mark a significant development given its military capabilities and strategic position along the Red Sea.
The country has also been considering joining a mutual defence pact involving Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Türkiye, signed in August.
Abdelatty said earlier this month that Egyptian membership remained “under serious consideration.”
A history of involvement in Yemen
Egypt joined the Saudi-led coalition supporting Yemen’s internationally recognised government in March 2015, primarily as a naval partner tasked with protecting Red Sea shipping lanes.
Cairo sent warships, pledged air support and deployed around 800 ground troops, although its direct combat role remained limited.
The country has a difficult history of military intervention in Yemen, having suffered heavy costs during its involvement in the 1960s. It has not undertaken a large-scale foreign ground deployment since the 1991 Gulf War.
Saudi Arabia remains a key political and financial partner for Cairo, providing billions of dollars in assistance, central bank deposits and energy supplies during Sisi’s presidency.
Red Sea security raises regional stakes
The latest escalation has added another volatile front to the wider US-Israeli war on Iran. The Houthis, who control Yemen’s capital, Sanaa, have attacked targets including Riyadh’s international airport and Saudi oil giant Aramco, disrupting flights and oil exports.
The conflict also threatens maritime traffic through the Bab al Mandab Strait, a strategic chokepoint for shipping travelling between the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden. Any sustained disruption could affect routes serving the Suez Canal, a major source of revenue for Egypt.
Saudi Arabia and Egypt have stepped up security discussions as the fighting intensifies. Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman visited Cairo on September 15 to discuss security and navigation in the Red Sea.
The extent of any Egyptian military support will depend on Saudi Arabia’s requests and how Cairo balances its security commitments with efforts to prevent further regional escalation.

high_priority_articles.title: Lula wins Brazil’s presidential election; Trump says vote looks ‘rigged’: Early analysis from Chatham House experts - Chatham House
high_priority_articles.summary: Lula wins Brazil’s presidential election; Trump says vote looks ‘rigged’: Early analysis from Chatham House experts  Chatham House
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, commonly known as Lula, has been re-elected president of Brazil for a fourth term. Lula secured 51.79 per cent of the vote against Bolsonaro’s 48.21 per cent.
The victory was a surprise: Lula’s opponent, Flávio Bolsonaro, led in the first round of the election held on 4 October. The result was announced after an unusual decision on Sunday by the country’s Supreme Court, which allowed polling centres to remain open longer than planned.
‘This, my fourth term, will be the best of any president in the history of this country’.
Defeated candidate Bolsonaro initially refused to accept the result, saying:
‘It is impossible to recognize the election results, given the circumstances under which things unfolded.’
A spokesman for Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party later said they accepted the result, but still had concerns about the election process. On Monday President Donald Trump said the election looked ‘rigged’.
Below, Chatham House experts provide analysis of the meaning of the result for Brazilians, the region and the world.
Eduardo Vasconcelos on Brazil’s Supreme Court
Dr Christopher Sabatini on what next for US relations?
Dr Bruno Binetti on Brazil’s China policy
Vanessa Rubio Marquez on the left and right in Latin America
Luis Miguel Castilla Rubio on Lula’s policies and Brazil’s economy
Lula’s victory and reform of the Supreme Court
Eduardo Vasconcelos, Academy Fellow, Latin America Programme
About 35,000 Brazilians voted after polls were due to close at 5PM on Sunday, most in the first five minutes as queues cleared. Only some 5,300 votes came after 5.05PM, when the Supreme Court’s two-hour extension could have made a difference.
Those few thousand votes may not have decided the election – Lula won by 4.4 million votes – but the extension of voting cost Brazil, as it gave Flávio Bolsonaro his pretext to question the result. Bolsonaro’s party has conceded defeat and Bolsonaro has refrained from disputing Lula’s victory. But he has still cast doubt on the process, saying ‘It was not me who lost, it was the system which won’.
On polling day, Lula’s campaign complained that buses had stopped running in several cities; Flávio’s team also asked for extra time in towns hit by heavy rain. The Superior Electoral Court was still weighing both requests when Lula’s campaign went to the Supreme Court. A single justice, Cristiano Zanin, extended voting nationwide minutes after polls had closed. Closed machines could not be reopened. In the same neighbourhood, one voter might still cast a ballot while another was turned away.
Zanin’s decision was the final act of a campaign season in which judges were called upon more than ever to set the terms of competition. By 21 October the electoral court had received 804 legal challenges over the presidential race, against 325 at the same point in 2022.
This has come at a time when the Supreme Court’s reputation is badly tarnished, after it failed to decide whether to investigate one of its own justices. Three in four Brazilians say its members have too much power. A record 48 per cent distrust it.
Brazil’s courts used extraordinary powers to protect the 2022 election from an authoritarian threat. After this election, the country now faces a new task. It must constrain the Court’s powers within ordinary limits, so that no single judge can change the rules on election day again.
Three reforms would help improve the Court’s reputation. Decisions that alter electoral rules or suspend laws passed by Congress should require the full Court. Justices should serve fixed terms. And misconduct cases against justices should be decided within set deadlines. Majorities of both Lula’s and Flávio’s voters back full-court decisions and fixed terms.
Lula may fill four seats on the Court by 2030. Each will need 41 Senate votes, giving senators leverage to demand reform. They must put aside squabbling to cohere behind voters’ wishes and compel reform of the system. Without it, trust in Brazil’s institutions may suffer even more.
What next for US relations?
Christopher Sabatini, Director of Chatham House’s Latin America Programme
While President Donald Trump claimed Brazil’s second round presidential election looked ‘rigged’ on Monday, other heads of state rushed to recognize President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s unexpected second-round presidential victory over conservative Flávio Bolsonaro.
French President Emmanuel Macron, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney all publicly congratulated Lula on his victory. Even Brazil’s more conservative neighbours joined the chorus, including Peruvian President Keiko Fujimori, Ecuadorian President Daniel Noboa, Chilean President José Antonio Kast, and Paraguayan President Santiago Peña.
The White House’s response is not surprising. It had been counting on the election of Bolsonaro to complete its bingo card of right-wing presidents in the Western Hemisphere, following a period of sustained electoral success for right-wing candidates stretching from Honduras to Argentina. But Latin American regional solidarity and respect for democratic institutions and the popular will trumped ideology and alignment with the US.
Adding Latin America’s largest democracy and economy would have represented a major victory for the self-proclaimed ‘Donroe Doctrine’. Instead, public support for Lula’s re-election may demonstrate that the bloc of Trump-aligned and Trump-adjacent presidents may not be as strong and ideological as many thought. (Only Argentine President Javier Milei has withheld congratulations for Lula.)
After initially calling for an annulment, members of the defeated candidate’s team said the party accepted the results but questioned the conditions of the election process. Unlike his father, Jair, did in 2022 when he lost to Lula, Flávio seems to be walking back an outright rejection of the election, while still undermining public confidence in the election results.
Their questions over how the situation unfolded hinges on a Supreme Court justice who supported Lula’s Workers’ Party request to extend voting by two hours on Sunday. That request was made originally by both parties to Brazil’s electoral court – in order to accommodate voters who struggled to make it to the booths due to heavy rains, and others allegedly affected by limited public transportation. But the decision to kick the request up to the Supreme Court after the electoral court failed to respond casts a pall over the results – and further threatens the reputation of a Supreme Court already under suspicion for being politicized.
Brazil’s modern, transparent voting system will be able to demonstrate the results – for those who want to believe them. But for core Bolsonaro supporters, trusting the results may be difficult. Flávio’s father also claimed unproven fraud in 2022. And father and son have baked distrust of the judicial and electoral system into their political DNA, polarizing politics and society in Brazil.
In the end, how far Flávio’s team decides to take its claims of fraud may depend on the White House and the US State Department. Both had a lot riding on a Bolsonaro victory. For Trump it would have been the crowning achievement for his support in the region, during this heavy year of presidential elections across the hemisphere.
For others the issue is more ideological and personal. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, like many Cuban-Americans, saw Lula’s Workers’ Party as complicit in upholding the communist regimes in Cuba and Nicaragua. Creating a ring of conservative, anti-communist governments across the hemisphere to stand with the US against those regimes has long been a dream of Republican administrations and Cuban-Americans in Florida. Their perspective will likely also help decide whether and when the Trump administration accepts a Lula victory.
With conservative majorities in both houses of Congress, Lula will have a difficult time attempting to tackle the economic and fiscal reforms necessary to keep the government solvent and address its looming sovereign debt. But the biggest loser in the election is social trust. The country’s voters are now almost evenly split between Bolsonaro and Lula (only 3.6 per cent separated the two leaders). And popular confidence in the Supreme Court may decline even more.
Will Lula change Brazil’s approach to China?
Bruno Binetti, Associate Fellow, Latin America Programme
Lula’s re-election, following a campaign in which he declared that Brazil was ‘nobody’s backyard’ and denounced foreign interference, will be welcomed in Beijing.
China retains a close partner in Latin America’s largest economy, at a time when most countries in the region have moved closer to the Trump administration. Lula shares China’s commitment to a multipolar international order with a stronger role for the Global South. That includes efforts within BRICS to reduce reliance on the US dollar in international trade, reform global financial institutions and expand climate finance for developing countries.
This partnership is underpinned by strong economic ties – ties so important they would have endured a Bolsonaro victory. China has been Brazil’s largest trading partner since 2009, driven by Brazilian exports of soybeans, iron ore and crude oil. In 2025, Brazilian exports to China reached $100 billion, compared with $38 billion to the US. This makes continued engagement with Beijing a priority for the powerful agribusiness sector, which is well represented in Congress and traditionally aligned with Bolsonaro and the political right.
Brazil was also the world’s largest recipient of Chinese investment in 2025, with Chinese firms expanding their presence in electricity infrastructure, manufacturing and mining. In the automotive sector, BYD and Great Wall Motor have established electric vehicle production facilities in Brazil, and Lula is pushing Chinese manufacturers to use more local suppliers and create jobs.

high_priority_articles.summary: France's debt woes in focus as ECB meets | Gulf Times  Gulf Times
high_priority_articles.full_text:
France's deteriorating public finances will take centre stage when the European Central Bank (ECB) meets this week, but policymakers are not expected to throw a lifeline to the eurozone's second-biggest economy just yet.
The ECB is set to keep interest rates on hold, having already hiked them twice this year, walking a fine line between tamping down inflation fuelled by the Iran war energy shock and supporting the eurozone economy.
But the focus of Thursday's meeting is likely to shift quickly to France and "how the ECB will respond to the ongoing fiscal and political crisis," said Andrew Kenningham, chief Europe economist at Capital Economics.
French bond yields, which reflect the cost of government borrowing, surged to their highest level since 2002 last week amid a standoff over next year's budget, which aims to reduce the country's vast debts.
Concerns have also been fuelled after protests, driven in part by demands for more spending on public services, degenerated into the worst street violence in years.
There has been speculation that the ECB could, for the first time, use a crisis-fighting tool aimed at combatting sharp movements in markets to push down French bond yields.
However, the criteria to activate the so-called Transmission Protection Instrument (TPI) are strict, and most observers believe France's problems do not meet the threshold.
The ECB stipulates that the tool can only be used to counter "unwarranted" moves in markets, where there is a risk of financial stress spreading -- but not in cases where problems stem from poor fiscal policy.
So far ECB President Christine Lagarde, who also once served as France's finance minister, has sounded cool about the idea.
Asked about France's rising yields earlier this month, she responded: "The primary and first solution lies at home in France. And it has to do with fiscal policies."
France's central bank chief, who sits on the ECB's governing council, also downplayed the prospect of an intervention, saying that "conditions are not met" for the central bank to step in.
Kenningham of Capital Economics predicted there would be "no lifeline for France" at Thursday's meeting, saying spreads between French and German bonds, the eurozone benchmark, would need to widen far more to justify any action.
Despite rising inflation caused by higher energy prices, the central bank for the 21 nations that use the euro is expected to keep its benchmark rate steady at 2.5%.
The ECB's rate call will come a day after the Federal Reserve announces its latest decision, with the US central bank also expected to stay on hold following a hike in September.
Eurozone inflation rose to a three-year high of 3.8% in September, although closely watched core inflation -- excluding volatile energy and food prices -- hardly changed.
There have so far been "very little knock-on effects from higher energy prices," ING economist Carsten Brzeski told AFP.
And France's crisis had "actually lowered chances of another rate hike," he said, adding that the "bond markets have taken over the ECB's task".
Rising bond yields cause tighter financing conditions and can push up borrowing costs for businesses and households, similar to the impact of higher rates.
Most economists predict the ECB will make the final hike of its current tightening cycle in December when it will be armed with updated growth and inflation forecasts.
Lagarde is also likely to face questions about her future as speculation intensifies she will step down before her term as ECB chief officially ends in October next year.
She has been linked to the top job at the World Economic Forum, which hosts a gathering of the global elite every year in the Swiss Alps resort of Davos.
But she has been tight-lipped so far, saying at the ECB's last meeting in September there was "nothing to report" on the matter.

high_priority_articles.title: South Korea's KOSPI Breaches 6,000 Intraday as SK Hynix's $74.8 Billion Shareholder Return Plan Fuels Semiconductor Rally - BigGo Finance
high_priority_articles.summary: South Korea's KOSPI Breaches 6,000 Intraday as SK Hynix's $74.8 Billion Shareholder Return Plan Fuels Semiconductor Rally  BigGo Finance
high_priority_articles.full_text:
South Korea's KOSPI climbed back above the 6,000 mark intraday for the first time in 10 trading days, driven by a flood of buying into large-cap semiconductor stocks after SK Hynix unveiled record quarterly results and a 100 trillion won (approximately $74.8 billion) shareholder return plan. The index surged as much as 6% before giving back some of its gains in late morning trading and slipping back into the 5,900s.
According to the Korea Exchange on Oct. 28, the KOSPI hit 6,003.22 at around 10:57 a.m., up 6.47% from the previous session, breaching the 6,000 level. The index opened at 5,763.85, up 2.23% from the prior day, and quickly extended its advance. As of 11:04 a.m., it stood at 5,993.49, up 355.15 points, or 6.3%. The move followed a 3.09% gain the previous day, marking a second consecutive session of sharp gains.
As the rally accelerated, a buy-side circuit breaker was triggered on the main KOSPI market for a second straight day. At 9:54:24 a.m., when the KOSPI 200 futures index rose 5.17% to 928.02 from the previous close, program trading buy orders were suspended for five minutes. It was the first back-to-back buy-side circuit breaker since July 21-22, roughly three months ago.
SK Hynix was at the center of the day's rally. The company disclosed before the market opened that its third-quarter consolidated revenue came in at 104.6155 trillion won (approximately $78.3 billion) and operating profit at 83.3334 trillion won (approximately $62.3 billion), both all-time highs. Its operating margin reached 79.7%. The company also announced a large-scale shareholder return program that includes more than 60 trillion won (approximately $44.9 billion) in share buybacks and cancellations and more than 30 trillion won (approximately $22.4 billion) in cash dividends. The plan calls for returning most of the gains from its Kioxia investment this year to shareholders; combined with the 40 trillion won (approximately $29.9 billion) approved in August, total shareholder returns for the year will reach 100 trillion won.
Buying intensified during an earnings briefing held mid-session, where the company confirmed that demand for DRAM and high-bandwidth memory (HBM) remains solid. SK Hynix traded up 9.1% at around 1.45 million won (approximately $1,100) intraday, while SK Square also showed strength, gaining about 9%.
Samsung Electronics also jumped about 8%, reclaiming the 240,000 won (approximately $180) level. The gain was seen as front-running expectations for the company's finalized third-quarter results and shareholder return announcement scheduled for Oct. 29. Samsung Electronics preferred shares and Samsung Electronics both rose around 9%, while Samsung C&T gained 8.97% and Samsung Life Insurance climbed 9.41%. By sector, electrical and electronics led with an 8.25% gain, followed by insurance (7.0%), securities (6.02%) and distribution (5.22%). Only real estate (-0.1%) and paper and wood (-0.17%) posted slight declines.
Foreign investors and institutions drove the buying. On the main KOSPI market, foreigners net bought 639.8 billion won (approximately $478.7 million) and institutions net bought 596.4 billion won (approximately $446.2 million), while retail investors net sold 1.2346 trillion won (approximately $923.7 million), taking profits.
A tailwind from Wall Street overnight also lent support. Tech stocks drew buyers on news that AI company Anthropic filed for an initial public offering and on a large-scale AI equipment financing deal, pushing the Nasdaq Composite up 1.18% to close at 26,477.81 and the S&P 500 up 0.60% to 7,722.60. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index jumped more than 3%.
The KOSDAQ rose in tandem. At the same time, the KOSDAQ index stood at 769.86, up 26.03 points, or 3.5%, from the previous session. It opened up 1.76% and widened its gain to around 3%. Retail investors and institutions net bought 1.5 billion won (approximately $1.1 million) and 72.6 billion won (approximately $54.3 million), respectively, while foreigners net sold 68 billion won (approximately $50.9 million). Robot-related stocks stood out, with Rainbow Robotics surging 14.94% and Robotis jumping 9.76%, while Jusung Engineering (5.09%) and Ecopro (3.09%) also advanced.
In the Seoul foreign exchange market, the won-dollar exchange rate was trading at 1,335.8 won as of 11:30 a.m.
The surge comes as concerns over AI profitability that had been weighing on the semiconductor sector have eased. Anthropic's push toward a listing, Broadcom's large-scale chip contract and the strong reception to Meta's stock offering have successively lifted investor sentiment, with SK Hynix's earnings and return plan serving as the catalyst, analysts said.
Kim Dong-won, head of research at KB Securities, said, "At a time when semiconductor stocks are posting record earnings while trading at historically low valuations, the unprecedented expansion of shareholder returns at Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix is expected to be a decisive trigger for resolving undervalued corporate value."
Whether the rally can be sustained remains uncertain. Rate outlooks are murky ahead of the U.S. Federal Open Market Committee meeting, and it remains to be seen whether foreign net buying, now in its second day, will continue. The index's retreat from 6,000 back into the 5,900s intraday is also read as a sign of volatility stemming from short-term overheating.

high_priority_articles.title: South Korea's 1.0% Growth Surge Driven by Semiconductors - 조선일보
high_priority_articles.summary: South Korea's 1.0% Growth Surge Driven by Semiconductors  조선일보
high_priority_articles.full_text:
South Korea’s third-quarter economic growth rate surpassed expectations for the third consecutive quarter, driven by sustained increases in semiconductor exports amid a U.S.-led AI (artificial intelligence) boom. The Bank of Korea announced on the 27th that the country’s real gross domestic product (GDP) grew by 1.0% quarter-on-quarter in the third quarter. This figure is more than three times the central bank’s August forecast of 0.3%. Year-on-year growth reached 3.4%, also exceeding the projected 2.6%. If this momentum continues until year-end, annual growth could approach 4%, far surpassing the Bank of Korea’s forecast of 3.3%. Lee Dong-won, head of the Economic Statistics Department 2 at the Bank of Korea, stated, “Even if fourth-quarter growth is 0%, the annual growth rate would reach approximately 3.6%. If quarter-on-quarter growth exceeds 1.4%, an annual growth rate of 4% is possible.”
Similar to the first and second quarters, exports grew by 2.3% quarter-on-quarter, led by semiconductors and other IT products, marking a higher increase than the second quarter’s 1.3%. Year-on-year export growth was 8.6%, slightly lower than the second quarter’s 8.9%. Equipment investment increased by 4.1% quarter-on-quarter and 9.4% year-on-year, driven by rising investments in semiconductor facilities. Lee Dong-won explained, “Approximately half of the overall growth originated from semiconductors.”
Despite high growth driven by exports, private consumption contracted by 0.2% quarter-on-quarter, the first decline since the fourth quarter of 2022 during the COVID-19 pandemic. In the second quarter, private consumption had increased by 0.4% due to a stock market rally and Samsung Electronics’ gift certificate redemption event, which boosted home appliance purchases. However, this effect dissipated in the third quarter. Lee Dong-won noted, “The decline was influenced by reduced brokerage fees due to falling stock market trading volumes and delayed deliveries of completed vehicles caused by strikes at passenger car manufacturers. We expect private consumption to rebound in the fourth quarter as dividend payments from semiconductor firms and performance bonuses in the first quarter of next year increase household income.” The Bank of Korea added, “Consumption of goods such as passenger cars and home appliances, as well as services like finance and food, all decreased.” Year-on-year private consumption growth was 1.1%. Government consumption rose by 1.9% quarter-on-quarter and 2.6% year-on-year, driven by increased spending on goods and health insurance benefits.
The third-quarter real gross domestic income (GDI), which reflects export prices, surged by 3.4% quarter-on-quarter due to skyrocketing semiconductor prices amid global AI development competition. While this marked a slight decline from the previous quarter’s 3.7%, it remained over three times higher than GDP growth. Year-on-year GDI growth reached 18.8%, the highest since the fourth quarter of 1977. Unlike GDP, which measures domestic production, GDI is calculated by applying the price of exports relative to imports. Although the Middle East war pushed up import oil prices, semiconductor export prices rose more sharply, sustaining high GDI growth. The gap between GDI and GDP growth widened by 15.4 percentage points year-on-year, setting a new record for the third consecutive quarter.
With inflation persistently exceeding the Bank of Korea’s 2% target and growth remaining strong in the third quarter, the likelihood of an additional benchmark interest rate hike within the year has increased. The central bank had frozen rates on October 22 after raising them twice in July and August. Governor Shin Hyun-song views the high growth driven by the “semiconductor effect” as a demand-side inflationary factor. Following the rate freeze, he stated at a press briefing, “Given that growth and inflation trends are stronger than August’s projections, maintaining the current tight monetary policy stance is necessary.” The next Monetary Policy Board meeting, the last of the year, is scheduled for November 26.

source_detail.name: THE ELEC, Korea Electronics Industry Media

high_priority_articles.full_text:
Spanish semiconductor metrology equipment maker Wooptix plans to supply its Phemet wafer metrology system to a South Korean semiconductor manufacturer. The company will begin evaluating the equipment’s suitability for customer processes next year, aiming to enter mass-production lines within two to three years. Samsung Ventures led an investment in the company last year.
“We will begin deploying equipment at customer sites next year to validate its suitability for their processes,” said Marco Franchi, technical marketing manager at Wooptix. “Our goal is to enter mass-production lines within two to three years.” He did not disclose the customer’s identity.
“South Korea is a major market, home to Samsung Electronics and SK hynix,” Franchi said. “We plan to secure logic semiconductor customers in Korea before expanding into memory.”
Phemet is an automated metrology system that measures the shape of 300-millimeter wafers, including bow and warpage. It captures an image of an entire wafer in less than one second and offers subnanometer height measurement resolution. The system illuminates the wafer with light-emitting diodes (LEDs) and calculates its surface profile from phase differences in reflected light. Wooptix calls the technology Wavefront Phase Imaging (WFPI), which applies adaptive optics technology used in astronomical telescopes to correct atmospheric distortion. The company unveiled Phemet in November 2025 and installed its first system at French semiconductor research institute CEA-Leti in May.
Wooptix is targeting logic semiconductor manufacturers first because of increasing process complexity. Wafer alignment and shape control have become more challenging with gate-all-around (GAA) transistors and backside power delivery network (BSPDN) processes. The company subsequently plans to expand into advanced packaging applications, including hybrid bonding, as well as memory semiconductors.
“Metrology can determine whether wafers are misaligned during bonding and whether the bonding process has been completed properly,” Franchi said. “In the longer term, we are also considering miniaturizing the equipment for die-to-wafer (D2W) and die-to-die (D2D) processes.”
Founded in 2016, Wooptix raised more than 10 million euros in a Series C funding round in February 2025, jointly led by Samsung Ventures and the Spanish Society for Technological Transformation (SETT). Existing investors, including Intel Capital and Tokyo Electron (TEL) Venture Capital, also participated.
Wooptix is headquartered in Tenerife, Spain, where it also operates manufacturing facilities, and maintains offices in Madrid and Grenoble, France. About 60% to 70% of its approximately 80 employees work in research and development. The company plans to expand its workforce to around 100 by the end of this year or early next year.

high_priority_articles.summary: West warns of famine risk in Sudan as civil war grinds on  BBCUS, European powers warn of worsening hunger crisis in Sudan as over 5 million face food insecurity  Business Insider AfricaUS, dozens of countries warn of Sudan famine risk, urge aid  ReutersA War-Torn Nation Is on the Brink of Famine  NewserFood and Hope in Sudan  Send Relief
high_priority_articles.full_text:
The US and 30 other Western states have warned of an "alarming deterioration" in food security in Sudan, urging the warring sides in the civil war to remove obstacles to humanitarian aid to prevent famine.
In a joint statement, the signatories said conflict was the main driver of Sudan's hunger crisis, damaging critical infrastructure and disrupting food production.
"There is very little to survive on," Yusuf Roble, regional director for Islamic Relief East Africa, told BBC Newsday, describing how people returning to Omdurman were finding their homes destroyed or looted.
The war, which began in April 2023, has displaced 14 million people.
The statement was signed by EU states, the UK, Canada, Switzerland and Norway, as well as the US, where it was published by the state department on Monday after first appearing on the European Civil Protection and Humanitarian Aid Operations website.
It estimates that 19.5 million people or 41% of Sudan's population are experiencing high levels of acute food insecurity, including five million facing emergency levels of hunger.
"I met a mother of seven children who doesn't really know the whereabouts of her husband for the last three and a half years and he was the breadwinner, the sole breadwinner for the family," Roble said.
While the war in Sudan has led to what the World Health Organization has described as the world's worst humanitarian crisis, Roble said only 40% of Sudan's 2026 humanitarian needs plan had been funded as of September.
"Their meals come from the community kitchen, which doesn't really even have very long-term support because of funding cuts," Roble added.
The joint statement warns that "the number of children suffering from severe acute malnutrition could exceed the projected 825,000" without immediate action.
The crisis is being exacerbated by what the signatories describe as systematic obstruction of aid and the effects of El Niño, which has reduced rainfall and increased drought across more than half of Sudan.
"The parties to the conflict bear primary responsibility for alleviating the suffering of the Sudanese people," the statement says, urging them to lift all impediments to humanitarian assistance and allow full, safe, rapid and unimpeded access.
In June, the UN-backed Integrated Food Security Phase Classification, a measure of the severity and magnitude of food crises, estimated that 5.1 million people in Sudan faced severe hunger.
The civil war in Sudan began in April 2023 following a power struggle between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces.

high_priority_articles.title: Fed expected to hold rates steady, but Warsh may point way to more hikes - CNBC
high_priority_articles.summary: Fed expected to hold rates steady, but Warsh may point way to more hikes  CNBCThe Fed Is Expected to Hold Rates Steady. Warsh Will Have to Explain Why.  The New York TimesFederal Reserve likely to skip rate hike despite elevated inflation  The Boston GlobeFederal Reserve expected to hold interest rates steady in last decision before midterm elections  Fox BusinessFederal Reserve to announce its latest interest rate move this week. Here's what economists ex...
high_priority_articles.full_text:
Federal Reserve officials enter this week’s policy meeting amid a critical debate over what the central bank can, should and will do to address an inflation problem that shows no immediate sign of going away.
When the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee does release its decision Wednesday, markets overwhelmingly expect no change in benchmark interest rates following September’s quarter percentage point rate increase.
Investors will be looking closely, though, for clues about future moves from policymakers, and Chairman Kevin Warsh in particular.
Brett Ryan, senior U.S. economist at Deutsche Bank, said he’ll be watching what Warsh will signal about future policy moves — something the Fed chairman has said he is highly reluctant to do as he seeks to move the central bank away from the “forward guidance” practice of most of the 21st century.
The chairman “is likely to signal that recent inflation data reinforce expectations from the September meeting that further tightening will likely be needed over time,” Ryan wrote in a note to clients. “However, skipping October allows officials more time to assess trends in the data.”
Recent inflation data has offered little respite from the price pressures that intensified earlier this year.
The consumer price index, a widely cited inflation barometer, showed the annual rate at 3.7% in September, driven largely by soaring energy prices. Even stripping out volatile gas and groceries costs, the core CPI pointed to a 2.6% rate — still well above the Fed’s 2% mandate and heading in the wrong direction after climbing 0.3 percentage point from August.
At the same time, recent economic data has shown the housing market struggling further under the pressure of mortgage rates above 7%. The labor market, meanwhile, has settled into a low-fire, low-hire pattern where layoffs are around their lowest levels since the late 1960s, while people out of work struggle to find jobs.
Calibrating policy under current conditions is complicated by Warsh’s push for a more mercurial Fed that avoids signaling where policy is heading, preferring for markets to take their own signals from incoming data.
A pause this month could give the Fed more time to assess what impact the prior rate hike had on the economy and financial conditions. However, signaling tighter policy could put more strain on the housing and labor markets. Warsh and his colleagues must show they are prepared to contain inflation while avoiding a premature commitment to how far or how fast rates will rise.
Essentially, the Fed can use its interest rate to influence inflation. It almost certainly will hold off doing so as it evaluates current conditions. Markets and economists, though, are at odds over what it should do.
The chance of a mistake under those circumstances is significant, according to Krishna Guha, head of economics and central bank strategy at Evercore ISI.
“It ought to be possible for Warsh – who is alert to market risks even though he professes not to like mollycoddling investors – to show a calming steady hand,” Guha said Monday in a note. “But there is material execution risk.”
For instance, the Fed’s lack of detail on how it sees the risks to its dual mandate of low inflation and full employment as well as how it views both the pace and tightening of monetary policy poses substantial challenges.
While inflation data has been hot, the unemployment rate has been fairly steady.
The Fed also weighs financial conditions when figuring policy. The Chicago Fed’s index of financial conditions has shown a slight tightening since the September hike, a product of stock market volatility, among other factors.
Recent chatter out of key Fed officials, such as Vice Chair Philip Jefferson and New York Fed President John Williams, points to the likelihood of hikes at every other meeting. But how far the Fed will need to go remains a mystery.
Guha interprets remarks Warsh gave to the World Bank and International Monetary Fund in Bangkok recently as aligning “with the central view” on the FOMC. In practice, that’s a Fed moving “at a deliberative and methodical baseline pace of once per quarter without prejudice to what it learns along the way and how far it might ultimately have to go and whether at some point later down the line it might need to speed up.”
“If inflation continues to disappoint and/or growth momentum fails to moderate, the Fed will add more hikes,” he added.
Trading in the fed funds futures market points to about a 10% chance that the FOMC will raise rates this week, but a better than 80% probability of an increase in December, according to the CME Group’s FedWatch tool. The market sees the likelihood of another hike in March 2027, then about a 50-50 chance of a final move before the end of next year.
To be sure, there’s considerable debate among economists on whether the Fed should be tightening policy at all. Citigroup economists, for instance, think easing inflation data in the months ahead will give the Fed reason to stay on hold and perhaps begin cutting next year, though the firm is forecasting a hike this December.
Mohamed El-Erian, chief economic advisor at Allianz, said he expects further increases but believes that’s a mistake as they will hurt vulnerable areas such as housing and worsen economic disparities.
“My sense is that the market is right in saying that they’ll do nothing. [Warsh] will have to package it in quite a hawkish language because the [inflation] data all [have] come hotter than expected,” El-Erian said Monday on CNBC’s “Squawk Box.” “My problem is that it’s the wrong policy measure right now.”
The solution to worries about inflation and higher Treasury yields should be “fiscal containment, not monetary tightening,” he added.
“But we’re going to get monetary tightening, and it’s going to be what I call the one minus ‘X’ problem. ‘X’ is tech; it won’t be impacted that much,” El-Erian said. “It’s going to be the rest of the economy: housing, consumer car loans, consumer loans. That’s what’s going to be hit.”
Correction: Warsh gave remarks to the World Bank and International Monetary Fund in Bangkok. An earlier version misstated the name of one of the organizations.

high_priority_articles.full_text:
EU Greenwashing Rules Push Lufthansa to Swap Green Fare Name for Impact Fare
- New fare name: Lufthansa Group is renaming its Green Fare, launched in 2023, to Impact Fare.
- Regulatory driver: The company cited new rules on environmental communication without naming the regulation.
- SAF funding: Each booking funds extra SAF equal to 10-20% of a flight’s estimated emissions.
Lufthansa Group is renaming its Green Fare to Impact Fare. The fare lets passengers fund emissions reduction and removal, and more than 5 million have booked it since 2023. The company cited “new regulatory requirements for environmental communication” as the driver for the change.
For every Impact Fare booking, Lufthansa Group deploys extra Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF), a lower-emission jet fuel. It does so within six months of departure. On flights within Europe, the SAF volume is based on 20% of the flight’s estimated CO2 emissions. The remaining 80% sets a contribution to climate projects that avoid or remove CO2 outside the company’s value chain.
On intercontinental routes, the ratio is 10% to 90%. Customers can book the fare in all travel classes, and they receive extra Miles and Points. The group did not disclose the fare’s price or when the new name takes effect. “The new name places even stronger emphasis on customers’ contribution to greater sustainability in aviation,” the company said.
Regulatory Backdrop
The rename closely follows the start of application of the EU’s Directive on Empowering Consumers for the Green Transition (ECGT). The directive targets misleading green claims and other greenwashing practices. It also bans unverified generic claims such as “environmentally friendly” or “biodegradable.”
Last year, Lufthansa and other airlines agreed with the European Commission to stop using claims that national consumer authorities saw as misleading. These included claims that paying extra fees for climate projects or SAF could offset flight emissions. The deal followed a complaint by the European Consumer Organisation (BEUC), a consumer advocacy group. BEUC also asked authorities to make airlines refund green fees paid on the basis of misleading claims.

Why It Matters
The fare is one of Lufthansa Group’s five approaches to lower-emission aviation, alongside fleet renewal, fuel efficiency, SAF use and intermodality. It serves private and corporate customers who want to fund extra sustainability measures. If the new name satisfies the tighter claims rules, Lufthansa could keep selling passenger-funded SAF to corporate travel buyers.
